#3615. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Spain.

#3614. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3612. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3611. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

#3610. Paramount’s 4-Part Action Fantasy Epic Has One of the Best Seasons in TV History

With one of the best villains of all time

Few things feel more grown-up than dealing with the consequences of your actions. Whether you stay up too late and still have to get up the next day or make a mistake at work and have to answer for it, adulthood means no one’s coming to fix things. For the most part, it’s all up to you.

The Legend of Korra has been the subject of much criticism over the years, but it’s always been a show about its young hero Korra (Janet Varney) growing from a feisty teen into a relatively less feisty adult. It’s not until season 3 that she experiences her biggest change, dealing with the consequences of one of her biggest decisions: leaving the spirit world portals open.

It’s one of the best decisions Korra makes, but it also creates her most thought-provoking villain.

Season 3 is appropriately titled “Book 3: Change,” and it picks up after the Harmonic Convergence, the planetary alignment that flooded the world with spiritual energy. After a great battle (literally, Korra becomes a kaiju via astral projection), Korra leaves the portals open, believing that people and the spirits should live in harmony together. It’s a decision with vast ramifications, from spirits adorably popping up throughout Republic City to the awakening of air-bending skills in random people, reviving a culture that had been nearly lost.

One of these new benders is Zaheer (Henry Rollins), a member of the Red Lotus, which is a secret anarchist organization whose mission is to disrupt world order and eliminate the Avatar cycle. Zaheer uses his airbending to escape his high-security prison and rescue his comrades, who are some of the coolest villains in animation. These include the lavabender Ghazan (Peter Giles), waterbender Ming Hua (Grey DeLisle), and combustion bender P’li (Kristy Wu).

Meanwhile, Korra and her team travel the world, slowly collecting new airbenders in the hopes of rebuilding the Air Nation.

“Change” is a blockbuster of a third season, taking full advantage of Studio Mir’s animation capabilities. It’s the one season the studio animated from start to finish, and it shows. While The Legend of Korra always had incredible fights, in this season, the bending takes center stage. Ming Hua offers a new flavor of waterbending; she doesn’t have arms, so she fashions several out of water, looking like a terrifying spider. P’Li’s combustion is accompanied by a high-pitched whine, with the energy launching like a rocket through her third eye. Her hair is braided, and she’s huge. On a design level, these are the types of characters you only need to see once to remember forever.

Increasing the sense of peril is the fact that the Red Lotus feels so adult and experienced when compared to Korra and her friends. Zaheer and P’Li are devoted partners. Together, these four are close comrades, with their experiences and crimes weathered on their skin. It results in some of the franchise’s best showdowns, often involving characters that were previously sidelined, like Tenzin (J.K. Simmons), who has a standout battle in the Air Temple, and Korra’s father Tonraq (James Remar), who comes to her aid and prevents her from being kidnapped by the Red Lotus.

Then there’s Zaheer himself. He is a blank slate, the quietest and least charming member of a gang of incredibly cool villains. He’s so detached from the world and so at home with his ideologies that he feels inaccessible — no one’s convincing this guy of anything. His one tether to the world is P’Li, a relationship that the season cashes in on in spectacular fashion.

In arguably one of the coldest moments in kids' animation, Zaheer kills the Earth Queen by taking the air out of her lungs. Her death throws Ba Sing Se into chaos. And while the series never backs away from his extremism, like every great villain, Zaheer makes a lot of sense. His beliefs cause Korra to wonder if maybe the world would be better off without corrupt leaders like the Earth Queen, who lives surrounded by obscene wealth and imprisons her subjects for her own gain while the people in her kingdom suffer.

When it comes to Korra, there’s so much breathing room when the show finally drops her love triangle with Mako (David Faustino) and Asami (Seychelle Gabriel). It’s a development that allows Korra to focus on other things, like how bad she is at talking to bureaucrats or her having to hold back when speaking with people that are incredibly annoying.

Revenge is a dish best served 12 years later

Korra gets to explore her dynamics with other characters, including Suyin (Anne Heche) and Lin Beifong (Mindy Sterling), two standouts in the franchise. She’s also frequently paired with Asami, with the two finally moving past the fact that they dated the same guy (even if they’ll end up falling in love with each other the following season).

“I think Korra was more likable in Book 3 because — but that was actually part of her arc that we’d set out to do — is that she was becoming more selfless, and it wasn’t just about her own stuff,” co-creator Bryan Konietzko told The Mary Sue in 2014.

By the end of the “Change,” Korra has saved the world once more, but is more depleted than ever. After being poisoned by the Red Lotus, she’s in a wheelchair, watching her past self’s civilization restored as the Air Nomads rise once more. Another adult lesson Korra learns? Sometimes life’s greatest moments are bittersweet.

The Legend of Korra is streaming on Paramount Plus

When we received word that Marvel wasn’t moving forward with its Blade reboot starring Mahershala Ali, I have to be honest with you - I wasn’t heartbroken.

Now, this has nothing to do with the actor. I love Mahershala Ali. He’s super talented, and even though Blade isn’t moving forward, he’s still gotten rave reviews for other projects. Truth be told, the two-time Oscar winner has a right to be crestfallen, but he’ll be fine. Somebody as talented as he is will always land on his feet.

Even so, the reason why I wasn’t upset is that we still have Blade - and his name is Wesley Snipes. I know Feige and crew wanted to revamp the character, but why bother when Snipes is still kicking? I’ll explain.

We're two years removed from Deadpool & Wolverine, but can I just say that I still get giddy at all of the cameos in that film, namely Gambit, played by Channing Tatum, and Blade, played by Wesley Snipes. Their involvement was so cool, and I can attest that the biggest pop the movie got when I saw it back in 2024 was when Snipes stepped out of the shadows as Blade.

That’s because people LOVE Blade, especially Snipes’ rendition of him. This just got me thinking, though, because in the Avengers: Doomsday trailer, we clearly see Tatum’s Gambit fighting with Simu Liu’s Shang-Chi. So, if Gambit can return from Deadpool & Wolverine, why can’t Blade?

Granted, I don’t know if Blade is actually in the movie. Anything is possible right now with Doomsday's cast, but even if he’s not, why can’t Snipes return? I mean, the Fox X-Men are returning, including the late Patrick Stewart (RIP, Professor X). So why can’t Fox’s Blade return in his own new movie? That’s right. I’m talking Blade freaking Four, people! Don’t you think the Daywalker is due for another film? Because come on…

Unlike a lot of people, I don’t hate Blade: Trinity. In fact, like I said a number of years ago: Blade: Trinity is The Godfather Part III of superhero movies, and that’s okay. What I meant by that was, it’s fine, but it will always be in the shadow of its two superior predecessors. Blade: Trinity is just super forgettable, no matter how you slice it.

Should Blade really go out like that? I personally don’t think so. In the third film, we got some new characters: Whistler’s daughter, played by Jessica Biel, and Hannibal King, played by Deadpool actor Ryan Reynolds. That said, I honestly think these characters could just be ignored if there were ever a fourth film.

In fact, I think it would be pretty cool if a fourth Blade movie had the character surviving the Void in Deadpool & Wolverine, just like Gambit. He’d be scarred, of course, but still on the move, and I think the film could conclude with a proper ending for the character. Come on. You know you want it.

I was actually inspired to write this after going to a Halloween party. A good friend of mine was talking about Blade as if the movies had just come out yesterday, and I could tell that others still love and appreciate the character just as much as I do.

Also, it’s a shame that Blade kind of fizzled out after Blade: Trinity, even though he pretty much jump-started Marvel movies back in 1998. I mean, without the success of Blade, we might not even have the MCU today.

So, let’s bring Wesley Snipes back into the MCU. Come on. You know you want him.

Roborock’s Qrevo 2 Pro robot vacuum and mop is down to $649.98 at Amazon (regularly $899.99)—a $250 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers—making it a solid mid-range option for homes with a mix of carpets and hard floors. Its 25,000Pa suction is designed to pick up everything from crumbs and dust to pet hair, while the anti-tangle brushes help keep long hair from wrapping around the rollers. More importantly, it automatically detaches its mop heads at the dock before vacuuming carpets, so you don't have to worry about damp rugs as it moves between different floor types.

As for how well it cleans, its mopping performance is excellent, with its maximum water flow and cleaning settings managing to lift even dried-on ketchup, though this mode is slow and leaves floors fairly wet. Vacuuming is generally good, too, especially on carpets. That said, you'll want to consider the clearance beneath your furniture, as the LiDAR sensor mounted on top gives this robot vacuum a relatively tall profile that prevents it from reaching under low furniture.

That limitation aside, much of the day-to-day upkeep is handled by the multifunctional dock, which automatically empties the dustbin, refills the robot’s water tank, washes the mop heads, and dries them with warm air. You'll still need to refill the dock's clean water tank, empty the wastewater, and replace the dust bags periodically, but that's considerably less hands-on work than maintaining a basic robot vacuum and mop. And to give you more control over the Qrevo 2 Pro, the Roborock app lets you map individual rooms, set no-go zones, and schedule targeted cleaning, while support for Alexa, Google Home, and Matter allows you to integrate it into your existing smart home setup.

#3606. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

When I think about the challenges that may have come with making Wicker, the wicker itself and the sheer horniness of the film (which the reviews pointed out) come to mind first. This project on the 2026 movie schedule required Alexander Skarsgård to be covered in wicker the whole time, and he and Olivia Colman have some very intimate scenes throughout the film. It’d make sense if all that was tough to work through. However, when Skarsgård was asked if he thought it’d be difficult to play the Wicker Husband, his response about why it was surprised me.

While Olivia Colman has been open about filming sex scenes in Wicker and working with the intimacy coordinator to make them feel “easy,” Skarsgård opened up about a different challenge that came with this movie. During an interview with the NYT, he explained that playing such a pure character was "foreign" to him, and that was a hurdle he had to get over:

There was a purity there that felt foreign to me. [Laughs] I had come off a string of darker, morally corrupt characters, and there was something so pure and beautiful about this character. It was a bit, I won’t say scary, but playing the nice guy is slightly out of my wheelhouse. It’s easier to find something interesting in the darkness of a character.

Now, I don’t know about you, but the last movie I saw Alexander Skarsgård in was Pillion. Like Wicker, it’s a romance. However, that’s all they have in common, and that’s especially true when you compare Skarsgård’s characters. The beloved Wicker Husband is so kind, gentle, and open-hearted. Ray, the biker he plays in Pillion – which is a romance involving a BDSM relationship between Ray and Harry Melling’s Colin – is incredibly closed off, demanding, and cold. In short, Ray is anything but “pure and beautiful.”

Along with Pillion (which you can stream with an HBO Max subscription), Skarsgård’s most recent projects include the concert mockumentary The Moment, the sci-fi series Murderbot and the war movie Lee, to name a few. None of those are the fantastical romance Wicker is, so this new movie required the actor to tap into a different side of himself.

Plus, as he said, it’s not often we see him play a genuinely nice guy, and I wouldn’t say his career is defined by wholesome characters. So, I can see why this role in Wicker challenged him. While the Wicker Husband and Fisherwoman have a very R-rated sex life, they have a remarkably loving and, in many ways, wholesome relationship. And while it was a challenge for Skarsgård to play that out at first, he nailed it, and he said he loved the experience too.

Now, if you’d like to see Alexander Skarsgård play a significantly less dark character than he’s usually known for, you can catch Wicker in theaters now.

#3603. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3601. 10 Perfectly Designed Final Fantasy Magic Cards That Are 10/10, No Notes

A critical hit of Final Fantasy nostalgia

Magic: The Gathering's Final Fantasy crossover set is a love letter to one of gaming's most enduring franchises, bringing together characters, creatures, locations, and iconic moments from across the series' history. With 16 mainline games and even more when counting sequels and spinoffs, Wizards of the Coast had quite the challenge in translating decades of RPG storytelling into a card game with its own language and mechanics.

Packed with hilarious nods, like Suplex, and incredible powerhouses, like Diamond Weapon, it comes as no surprise that Final Fantasy is among the best Universe Beyond sets in the game. But the most perfect designs among them capture a fundamental element of their source material, whether that's Bahamut's devastating Mega Flare, Phoenix Down's clutch resurrection, or the sheer spectacle of summoning Primal Odin.

Whether through clever mechanics or an inspired bit of flavor, these 10 Final Fantasy cards represent the very best of what this crossover has to offer.

Sin anchors the legacy of Final Fantasy antagonists through crushing generational dread, and its card design captures that weight without relying on a lazy stat line. Whenever Sin, Spira's Punishment enters the battlefield or attacks, it exiles a random permanent card from your graveyard, creating a tapped token copy if it's a permanent and repeating the process if a land is hit. Sin is particularly nasty in Commander decks built around graveyard recursion and land synergies, especially when paired with cards like Adrix and Nev, Twincasters, which doubles the tokens it creates, or Hedron Crab, which helps stock the graveyard with fresh targets.

It's an unpredictable engine that turns the remnants of your battlefield into compounding threats throughout the game. Spira’s Punishment also evokes the inescapable cycle of destruction and rebirth that defines Final Fantasy 10, where Spira's people have endured a thousand years of Sin's devastation, rebuilding their lives after each attack and relying on Summoners to temporarily defeat the monster through a ritual sacrifice. Even its seven-mana cost feels entirely appropriate for a monster of its magnitude, though maybe 10 would’ve been more apropos.

Weapons in gaming rarely carry the instant recognition of Cloud Strife's enormous Buster Sword — whether you picture it crudely strapped to his back during the bleak industrial sprawl of early Final Fantasy 7 or dragging it through the mud in Remake — but its significance extends well beyond its imposing silhouette. Passed down through Angeal, Zack, and eventually Cloud, the sword represents the heavy burden of legacy and what one generation leaves behind for another.

Magic: The Gathering captures some of that history through its equipment design, with the Buster Sword giving its wielder a substantial power boost of +3/+2. Whenever said creature hits an opponent directly, you draw a card, then get the opportunity to cast a spell from your hand for free, provided its mana value doesn't exceed the damage dealt. It's a suitably devastating reward for landing a direct hit, and a fitting tribute to one of Final Fantasy's most enduring symbols.

At first glance, Cactuars look like little more than walking houseplants, but when crossed, they can hit you with a devastating flurry of needles. Among Final Fantasy's most recognizable recurring monsters, Cactuars have made a career out of looking harmless before delivering some devastating blows, similar to the goofy-looking Tonberries. MTG’s Jumbo Cactuar follows that lineage beautifully through a seven-mana creature with a relatively unassuming 1/7 stat line. It looks like any regular green common creature, until you notice its ability, 10,000 Needles, which gives it a whopping +9,999/+0 whenever it attacks.

That's right, this seemingly harmless plant suddenly becomes a 10,000-power monster capable of flattening just about anything in its path. It's an almost comically literal interpretation of the Cactuar family's signature attack, and that's what makes it so brilliant (and hilarious). There's no need for elaborate transformations or complicated synergies. Magic simply takes one of Final Fantasy's most recognizable monster abilities and turns it into a devastating combat trick.

While Final Fantasy 13 remains one of the most divisive entries in the franchise’s storied history, Lightning herself stands tall as one of its absolute finest protagonists. She’s a relentless soldier defined by unwavering resolve and immediate action, a former Guardian Corps sergeant who goes AWOL during the violent exile of Bodhum's citizens, derailing a Purge train and battling through the Hanging Edge to rescue her sister.

Her Magic card captures that uncompromising spirit right out of the gate. A three-mana creature with first strike, trample, and lifelink is already a formidable combatant, but her stagger ability is what makes the design sing. Whenever Lightning, Army of One deals combat damage to an opponent, all damage dealt to that player and their permanents by any source is doubled until your next turn. It’s a brilliant adaptation of FF13’s defining combat rhythm, where staggering an enemy leaves them completely exposed to devastating follow-up attacks. Magic turns her into the tip of the spear for an all-out assault, translating one of the series' signature mechanics into a game-winning tactical engine.

Zack Fair's story is one of Final Fantasy 7’s most heartbreaking, particularly because his final moments have such a profound impact on Cloud's journey. Magic honors the character with a 0/1 legendary creature that enters with a +1/+1 counter on it. You can play one mana to sacrifice Zack Fair and give another creature indestructible, Zack’s counters, and even the equipment attached to him.

It's a thoughtful piece of design that essentially turns his death into an act of protection and inheritance. There's no elaborate transformation or complicated combination of abilities, Zack's final act becomes a playable mechanic, allowing another hero to carry his strength and equipment forward. It’s hard to imagine a more poignant tribute to a character whose entire legacy is defined by passing the torch, and some players have found clever ways to abuse it by looping him from the graveyard with reanimation engines like Sun Titan or Lurrus, repeatedly granting their board indestructible while constantly passing his stat boosts down the line.

Aerith’s power has always stemmed from gentle resilience rather than overwhelming force. She’s a healer, after all, and the last surviving Cetra, hiding in plain sight selling flowers in the Sector 5 slums while carrying the solitary burden of the Planet's survival. In Magic, Aerith Gainsborough is a 2/2 legendary creature that enters the battlefield with lifelink, and whenever you gain life, she receives a +1/+1 counter. This makes her progressively stronger as she supports your other creatures and keeps your life total at a healthy advantage over your opponents.

However, the real stroke of genius comes when Aerith dies. Every legendary creature you control receives +1/+1 counters equal to the number Aerith had accumulated during her time on the battlefield. It's a beautiful mechanical interpretation of her legacy, particularly considering the profound impact her death has on Cloud and the rest of the party in the original game. Aerith's influence doesn't disappear when she's gone, but lives on through the people she leaves behind. And it’s even better when you’ve already got a 12/12 Eldrazi on the board.

Final Fantasy 10’s Yuna is a summoner first and foremost, making her one of the most natural candidates for a Magic card built around enchantments and their associated creatures. What makes Yuna, Hope of Spira particularly clever is how the card encourages players to assemble a collection of saga creatures, the special enchantments introduced in the Final Fantasy set to represent the franchise's iconic summons.

During your turn, Yuna grants herself and your other enchantment creatures trample, lifelink, and ward 2, making the entire group considerably more difficult to deal with. She can also return an enchantment from your graveyard to the battlefield at the end of your turn, but with a finality counter on it that prevents it from returning to the graveyard again. It's a fantastic representation of Yuna's role as a summoner, turning her into the centerpiece of an entire Aeon-focused strategy with enchantment creatures cards like Yojimbo, Bahamut, Knights of Round, and more.

Speaking of Knights of Round, it's as much a powerful Magic card as it is a legendary summon in the games. First appearing as the ultimate secret Materia in Final Fantasy 7, tucked away on the unmapped Round Island and requiring a Gold Chocobo just to reach, it calls forth 13 holy knights to rain down an unskippable two-minute-long assault of apocalyptic damage. It was the absolute pinnacle of endgame excess, forcing players to sit back and watch a cinematic spectacle unfold while Sephiroth’s health bar disintegrated.

Magic’s interpretation of it is every bit as theatrical. Designed as an eight-mana Saga creature, Knights of Round gradually builds an army by creating three 2/2 Knight tokens across each of its first four chapters. That’s twelve knights in total, before its fifth and final chapter delivers Ultimate End, buffing your entire board with +2/+2 and dropping an indestructible counter onto each of your creatures. It's a wonderfully patient piece of design that rewards players for waiting out the full summon sequence, turning that notoriously long animation into a looming, game-ending countdown your opponents can only watch in dread. Unless they’re in blue, of course.

Sephiroth’s transformation from celebrated First Class SOLDIER hero to the cold One-Winged Angel remains one of gaming’s most devastating character arcs. He wasn't just a villain; he was Shinra's ultimate hero whose sanity shattered the moment he uncovered his horrific origins inside the Nibelheim mansion: he was engineered from the alien calamity Jenova. He burned Nibelheim to the ground and began viewing humanity as mere parasites. His tragic fall shifted the entire scope of Final Fantasy 7 from an anti-corporate resistance story into an apocalyptic cosmic horror.

Magic imbues that journey onto a double-faced creature that grows more dangerous as the battlefield descends into chaos. On his front side, Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER allows you to sacrifice another creature whenever he enters or attacks, drawing a card in return. Meanwhile, whenever another creature dies, you drain one life from an opponent and gain one yourself. Once that second ability has resolved for the fourth time in a single turn, Sephiroth transforms into his One-Winged Angel form, granting an emblem that keeps the life-drain engine running permanently whenever creatures die. You can also even stack that with his second ability, letting you sac as many creatures as you like in exchange for that many card draws. It's an inspired way to represent Sephiroth's growing power, turning the battlefield into a ticking clock as his enemies fall around him.

Final Fantasy 11 has no shortage of formidable enemies, but few developed the same legendary reputation as Absolute Virtue. This optional superboss became infamous for its extraordinary durability and punishing difficulty, earning a reputation as one of the most frustrating encounters in the entire franchise. Absolute Virtue could repeatedly unleash powerful abilities borrowed from multiple player classes, including Benediction, which allowed it to restore enormous amounts of health just when victory seemed within reach. Its substantial passive regeneration made matters even worse, turning the encounter into an exhausting war of attrition that demanded meticulous coordination from an entire alliance of players. Some groups spent more than 18 hours attempting to defeat it, cementing its place in MMO history as one of gaming's most notorious boss encounters.

Magic distills its intimidating presence through an eight-mana 8/8 construction that can't be countered when it’s played, plus it has flying, of course. Even more terrifying is its secondary ability, which grants you protection from each of your opponents, effectively making you untouchable while Absolute Virtue remains on the battlefield. Opponents can’t attack you, target you with spells, or even enchant you. It's a fitting translation of a boss that once seemed practically impossible to defeat, forcing opponents to find a way around its defenses before they can even think about bringing it down.

The hosts and musical guests for SNL’s 52nd season have been pretty great so far amid the 2026 TV schedule, but the surprise guests have been even better. For the show’s Halloween episode, which was actually on the spooky holiday this year, Tom Hanks made a comeback as David S. Pumpkins, the “King of Halloween,” for the cold open. He was once again joined by Mikey Day, with a surprise cameo by Bobby Moynihan as his skeletal dancing companions, and it was perfect! Yet I really wish I could've been a fly on the wall when Hanks and Moynihan hung out before the surprise reprisal.

This was only David S. Pumpkins’ fourth appearance on Saturday Night Live since his debut in October 2016, but he is arguably one of the best recurring characters to come out of the series. It's crazy to think that it’s been a decade since that first Pumpkins sketch first made its debut, and that makes the recent reprisal even more insane. Moynihan spoke to Mashable about what it was like being with Hanks for going live on Halloween, and this sounds like a dream:

I don’t think we, as the three of us, realized until dress that we were going to be standing there for that long, because the first hour of getting there was just standing there in the hallway with Tom Hanks going, like, ‘Can you believe that we’re here 10 years later?’ Like, ‘Can you honestly believe that 10 years later, we are standing here in these costumes?’ Like, we were just laughing about how ridiculous it was.

There are plenty of recurring sketches on Saturday Night Live, and every once in a while, a sketch that hasn’t been seen in years makes a return. I can’t imagine what it was really like for the group to step back into those costumes again, four years after the last time the sketch was done. It sounds like the reprisal was just as sweet for them as it was to the fans. That aside, I really do envy Moynihan and Day for getting to spend some personal time with the great Tom Hanks.

To say that David S. Pumpkins has become popular would be an understatement. Back in 2017, Pumpkins got his very own Halloween special. It was animated, absurd, and a half-hour filled to the brim with on-brand ridiculousness. Fans have also edited Mr. Pumpkins into horror films, and I would love nothing more than to get a full-length movie of him and his friends. The latest appearance from Pumpkins saw him and his dancers appear as part of a spooky attraction before James Austin Johnson’s President Trump cut in.

Meanwhile, David S. Pumpkins’ dancing friend was not the only character Moynihan reprised last week. He stopped by the Weekend Update desk and played the beloved Drunk Uncle as well. As for why Drunk Uncle popped in, he wanted to share some thoughts about “beer winning the World Series,” or more specifically, the Milwaukee Brewers. In a fun twist, Brewers Christian Yelich and Brice Turang, along with manager Pat Murphy, also stopped by the desk.

I couldn't think of a better Halloween episode for SNL, and I love that David S. Pumpkins is still around. Of course, it's hard to say if or when fans might see Tom Hank's eccentric character again. But right now, I'm just pleased that he got to reprise the role alongside Bobby Moynihan and Mikey Day. Fans can look back at all the sketches by using a Peacock subscription to stream all seasons of Saturday Night Live.

#3598. 23 Years Later, Buddy The Elf's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote Ever

When "Elf" came out in 2003, it established itself as an immediate Christmas classic, and on the movie's 23rd anniversary, we want to celebrate a simple, effective line from this Will Ferrell comedy which is not only fun for the whole family, but which has stood the test of time.

Before we get to the line in question, though, let's go over the basics where "Elf" is concerned. Directed by Jon Favreau (the Marvel and Star Wars one, not the political guy) and written by David Berenbaum, who wrote the movie after an earlier project called "Christmas in New Jersey" failed to take flight, "Elf" stars Ferrell as Buddy the titular elf, a human who's raised at the North Pole by his adoptive elf dad, Papa Elf (Bob Newhart, who also narrates the film). When Buddy sets out to find his birth father on the magical, mystical island of Manhattan, he meets Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical and uptight publisher of children's books who isn't super interested in dealing with any large adult son, let alone one dressed like a Christmas elf who pours sugar on his spaghetti. Thankfully, Walter's wife and son, Emily and Michael (Mary Steenburgen and Daniel Tay), love Buddy, so he's accepted into the Hobbs household and ends up saving Christmas.

There are a lot of great "Elf" quotes — and we'll feature a bunch of them shortly — but the one I really want to center is one that expresses Buddy's worldview perfectly. So what is it?

While talking to his coworker and eventual girlfriend Jovie (Zooey Deschanel), Buddy, trying to get her to sing in public, tells her, "The best way to spread Christmas cheer is singing loud for all to hear." Not only is this just a nice, neat little rhyme, it's also the entire essence of the movie.

Sure, Buddy can be annoying, loud, and weird; a grown man in an elf costume is a concept that's great on screen and would be objectively terrifying in real life. (It adds to the cinematic hilarity and imagined real-life horror that Will Ferrell is well over six feet tall.) Still, Buddy's big heart and intense joy ends up making everyone believe in the magic of the holiday season — even Walter, who eventually accepts Buddy as his son and decides that he wants to spend more time with Emily and Michael in the process.

"Elf" is truly a movie about allowing yourself to indulge in joy and cheer, and this Buddy quote is basically the film's thesis. That's not the only quotable line from "Elf," though; there are so many others.

#3596. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

By now, basketball fans are surely aware that Ernie Johnson is leaving Inside the NBA after the 2026-2027 NBA season. Johnson made the announcement at the end of October, and fans and celebrities alike have since been honoring him. One of the most emotional tributes, though, came from Johnson’s longtime co-hosts, Charles Barkley, who spoke about the news during an episode of the talk show. I was already in my feelings over the on-air tribute but, now, that’s amped up a bit since I’ve heard Johnson’s first-hand account.

Johnson initially revealed his news in a social media video that eventually went viral on October 28, and he spoke about it again at the top of Inside’s broadcast that evening. Following that opening, Johnson teed up the show, as per usual, by introducing co-hosts Barkley, Kenny Smith and Shaquille O’Neal. When Johnson threw it to Barkley, however, he was misty-eyed and momentarily at a loss for words. Johnson admitted on The Dan LeBatard Show (as seen on YouTube) that he was surprised, saying:

I was concerned, at first, because the camera was on him and he wasn't saying anything, and he had to kind of — like he was struggling and I was like, 'Oh, what's going on here?' The moments don't get much better than that for me when I think about the last few days. Because look, I've said it before, you guys have heard me, we love each other. We've been together for so long. We would do anything for one another.

That night, when the camera was on him, the usually humorous Barkley took a few seconds to compose himself. He eventually recovered, simply saying, “That was tough,” in a low and solemn voice. “Sir Charles” then proceeded to give a truly warm tribute to Johnson, which beautifully summed up the 26 years they’ve worked together. Check out Barkley’s tribute, and those of Smith and O’Neal by watching the video below:

Months ago, Charles Barkley claimed he would retire after this season and, in the process of doing so, he let slip that Johnson was doing the same. Barkley voiced his desire for both him and his co-host to step away from the show together. Johnson didn’t immediately confirm his plans for weeks, leaving much uncertainty. In the video, Johnson explained that he wanted to step away from the show as a way of slowing down a bit in order to spend some time with his family and focus on other ventures. Johnson also said this of his on-air tribute:

It was emotional for me. I mean, I was holding it together all day long and it was like, ‘Oh, man. I'm watching Chuck struggle with this.’ But that just speaks to the relationship we all have.

Charles Barkley Shares More Thoughts On Retiring From Inside The NBA, And I’m Starting To Believe He’ll Do It This Time

Johnson began hosting Inside back in the fall of 1990 and, under his leadership, the show became a must-watch program for basketball devotees like myself. The “Godfather” has been present for the series’ biggest moments, including its move from TNT to ESPN last season. Considering the veteran broadcaster’s long tenure with the program, the notion of him no longer hosting is somewhat hard to think about. What’s more is that there’s still the question of whether Barkley will truly retire (this time) as he declared.

Whatever the case, ESPN is reportedly committed to Inside the NBA regardless of Ernie Johnson and Charles Barkley’s plans. I’m not sure I’m ready to think about the prospect of the show being with two of its key members. For now, though, I’m just relishing this final season with the core four and hoping it produces even more memorable moments like Barkley’s sentimental tribute.

#3594. One Of Daredevil's Most Important Characters Was Only Supposed To Appear Once

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you asked Marvel readers to name Daredevil's most important supporting character, many would answer Elektra Natchios, the sai-wielding ninja assassin and Matt Murdock's sometimes lover, sometimes foe. But she came fairly late into the publication of "Daredevil." Created by writer/artist Frank Miller, Elektra debuted in 1980's "Daredevil" #168. The issue details her past of falling in love with Matt in college. In the present, the two are reunited because Elektra's assassin job brings her into conflict with Daredevil.

Miller had been drawing "Daredevil" since issue #158. He asked "Daredevil" editor Dennis O'Neil for a chance to write the book, and he turned it around completely. Miller transformed "Daredevil" from one of Marvel's least popular comics into one of its best, as his hard-boiled writing and dynamic action made "Daredevil" feel unlike any other comic. (Miller soon did a similarly influential revamp of Batman, which is why Batman and Daredevil remain so similar.)

"Daredevil" #168 was Miller's first solo writing credit on the book. His cover (inked by Klaus Janson) depicts a lightning strike, a fitting image for what Miller would do for the comic. That lightning conceals Elektra in shadow, while Daredevil looks on in horror. "Once he loved her... now she is his most deadly enemy!" the cover declares. Between the cover's imagery and the story promised by that caption, how could you not pick up this comic?

But at the time, Miller didn't see Elektra as the key to overhauling "Daredevil." In a 1983 discussion with Comics Interview magazine, Miller explained, "I came onto ['Daredevil'] thinking I was doing a couple of fill-ins on the writing. I ended up taking over the series, [and] had a character who was only supposed to appear for an issue take over the series on me — Elektra."

Frank Miller named Elektra after the Greek myth of Electra, the daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra who killed her mother to avenge Clytemnestra's murder of Agamemnon. Elektra Natchios is also defined by the death of her father, a Greek ambassador murdered in a hostage situation during Matt and Elektra's college years romance.

"Daredevil" by Miller takes a lot from film noir, and an alluring but deadly woman from the hero's past is a noir hallmark. Miller had one particular noir story in mind: Will Eisner's crime comic strip "The Spirit," particularly a 1950 story that introduced Sand Saref, the Spirit's childhood girlfriend turned femme fatale. Elektra's backstory — in love with the hero, rejects the law after her father dies, becomes an international criminal — hits the same beats as Sand's. (Bringing this full circle, Miller directed a "Spirit" movie in 2008 featuring Eva Mendes as Sand Saref, but it received very bad reviews.)

In the 2003 documentary "The Men Without Fear: Creating Daredevil," Miller recalled that he had wanted to introduce a new type of superhero love interest with Elektra, i.e. one who jumps across rooftops with her man. "Why wouldn't [superheroes] be operatic in their romance the way they are in combat?" Miller asked.

Knowing Miller apparently thought he might get one chance to tell Elektra's story, it makes sense that "Daredevil" #168 tells a complete and tragic arc. Daredevil and Elektra clash over the same quarry, and Matt remembers his past with Elektra (a blatant retcon, one smoothed over by Matt's inner dialogue suggesting it's been too painful to think of Elektra since). The issue ends with Daredevil revealing he's Matt Murdock to Elektra, but they still live in different worlds now. He then vanishes into the night, leaving Elektra crying alone.

Frank Miller actually brought Elektra back in his very next issue, "Daredevil" #169, but that appearance writes her out. She enters Matt's apartment, sees he's involved with Heather Glenn, and leaves, once more heartbroken. As Miller settled in on "Daredevil," though, he brought Elektra back in issue #174 as a regular character.

From there, she fought alongside Daredevil against the evil ninja cult the Hand and was hired to kill her lover by Wilson Fisk, the Kingpin. Fisk's former assassin, Bullseye, didn't take kindly to being replaced, so he murders Elektra in the double-length "Daredevil" #181. Elektra's fate echoes previous deaths of Marvel Comics female leads (now called "fridging"), like Gwen Stacy in "Amazing Spider-Man" or Jean Grey in "X-Men."

Miller felt that Elektra had to die or else she'd become an "insipid character," and he managed to convince Marvel's reluctant then editor-in-chief, Jim Shooter. But in Miller's penultimate issue, "Daredevil" #190, Elektra is revived by the Hand — unbeknownst to Matt, who still believes Elektra lost to him.

Elektra's resurrection opened the door for her to return, like in Miller and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Elektra: Assassin" or Miller's "Elektra Lives Again." Miller later revised Matt and Elektra's past in the 1993 miniseries "Daredevil: Man Without Fear" (drawn by John Romita Jr.), retconning Elektra into a dangerous thrill-seeker from the start.

Nowadays, Elektra sits as a permanent fixture of Daredevil's world, played in live-action by Jennifer Garner and later Elodie Yung. The comic Elektra even became Daredevil herself during writer Chip Zdarsky's run on "Daredevil." That endurance is not what Miller had wanted, and he admitted Elektra slipping through his hands "stings like hell" in "Marvel Comics: The Untold Story." If there's one publisher that won't let a good character go, after all, it's Marvel Comics.

#3593. macOS 27.3 Golden Gate beta 1 now available, here’s what to expect

Following last week’s release of macOS 27.2, Apple has now kicked off the next round of beta testing with the first developer beta of macOS 27.3 Golden Gate. Here are the details.

It’s been an unusually eventful few weeks for Mac users. In addition to several security releases for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate lats week, with expanded language support for Siri AI and new conversation recall capabilities.

On the hardware side, Apple recently announced new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display “with Touch,” as Apple has been addressing it.

Now, Apple is rolling out the first developer beta of macOS 27.3 Golden Gate, which will possibly include support for additional Siri AI languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, as Apple has promised to expand availability by the end of the year.

macOS 27.3 also brings several new features to Safari, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and the ability to organize tabs using Siri AI. You can read more about those changes here.

The update also comes as Apple prepares to launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3. However, the company has confirmed that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

macOS 27.3 may also most likely include further under-the-hood refinements to the macOS interface to accommodate touchscreen input, building on the new gesture recognition tools introduced in macOS 27.2.
