#3592. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3591. 5 Best Western Movies That Take Place In One Location

From Alfred Hitchcock's "Rope" to Sidney Lumet's "12 Angry Men," some of the best movies ever made have taken place in a single location. Limiting a film's scope in such a way is an extremely effective method for distilling the artform down to its most essential parts: character and storytelling. That's no different with Westerns.

Western movies have often taken advantage of America's incredible landscapes. From the genre defining Western (that barely impacted the box office) "The Big Trail" to the similarly decade-spanning tale of the Prescott family in "How the West Was Won," Western filmmakers have frequently made the land on which the United States was built as a big a character as the people themselves.

But some of the best Western films ever made have also unfolded on a much smaller scale — usually a frontier town where the clash between lawlessness and civilization can play out in microcosm. We've even seen Westerns confined to a single room. Regardless, placing limits like these on any film often brings out the best in its creators, and that's certainly been the case for this list of the best Westerns that take place in one location.

If you're going to make a movie set in one location, why not make it hell? That is, why not set it in a Western small town that may or may not be a physical manifestation of the underworld? The movie that prompted John Wayne to write an angry letter to Clint Eastwood was a fairly modest affair — at least in terms of its scope. 1973's "High Plains Drifter" sees Eastwood once again saddle up as a mysterious stranger. But this particular version of the Western archetype that Eastwood plays is less an anti-hero and more a manifestation of otherworldly retribution, who arrives in the town of Lago, ostensibly to protect its residents. In reality, he's there to make them pay for their sins.

One of many Westerns directed by Eastwood, "High Plains Drifter" is set almost entirely within Lago, where the townspeople allow outlaws to whip a U.S. Marshal to death. Eastwood's ghostly gunslinger then emerges from the surrounding desert embodying a cosmic fury as unforgiving as the parched plains from which he arrived. His order to paint every building in Lago red is designed as a way to depict the shame which covers the townspeople, and it's one of the most striking images in all of Eastwood's filmography.

Eastwood is no stranger to more grandiose depictions of the Old West. But "High Plains Drifter" proved he didn't need varied landscapes to produce a powerful Western. With just a morally compromised frontier town, Eastwood managed to further define the revisionist ethos that dominated Westerns of the 1970s, intentionally subverting the genre and upsetting old hands like the Duke in the process. Its status as one of the great Westerns of the 1970s has only grown, and rightly so.

Quentin Tarantino took a big gamble making "The Hateful Eight," mainly because he shot it in inclement and unpredictable weather. But it was also somewhat of a gamble because it took place almost entirely in a small cabin and was nothing like Tarantino's previous Western, 2012's "Django Unchained."

The film focuses on eight strangers as they shelter from a blizzard in Minnie's Haberdashery, a stagecoach stopover in Wyoming. These aren't the societal archetypes who found themselves in similarly close quarters back in John Ford's "Stagecoach," however. This wretched octet comprises some of the nastiest individuals to ever roam the Old West. Unsurprisingly, trapping them in a small space for a couple hours results in a series of extremely selfish and violent acts.

"The Hateful Eight" doesn't always appear near the top of Tarantino film rankings. But the movie was never going to be bad considering its cast. Alongside frequent Tarantino collaborators and all-round Hollywood legends Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Tim Roth, and Michael Madsen, the ensemble included Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demián Bichir, and Western veteran Bruce Dern — the man who shot down John Wayne himself back '72. What's more, "The Hateful Eight" earned three Academy Award nominations: Best Supporting Actress (Jennifer Jason Leigh), Best Cinematography, and Best Original Score, with legendary composer Ennio Morricone winning in the latter category. As such, "The Hateful Eight" is easily one of the best Westerns set in one location, and the only entry on this list to play out mostly in one small room.

Directed by the great John Ford, who knew all too well the value of grouping characters together in a single space following his 1939 triumph "Stagecoach," "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" saw John Wayne and James Stewart collaborate on-screen for the first time. That alone ensured the film would fare well with audiences. But this now legendary Western was about more than the confluence of two major Hollywood careers.

It's significant that the town Shinbone — in which the film plays out — exists in an unnamed state. The town represents the frontier, which in the present day timeline of "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" has been transformed from a lawless land to a more civilized society. But as we discover near the end of the film, that transformation and the success of Stewart's Senator Ransom Stoddard has been built on a lie. Meanwhile, John Wayne's rancher Tom Doniphon is shown to have passed away at the very beginning, establishing a mournful, reflective tone to the film before it flashes back to tell its story of an outlaw felled by Doniphon's bullet and the man who took the credit. Ford appeared to be crafting a sober requiem for the Old West as he'd depicted it throughout his career, for which Shinbone and Wayne stood as symbols.

Interestingly enough, "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" was literally restricted location-wise, having been shot mostly on Paramount sound stages. That coupled with Ford's decision to film in black and white makes the feature feel confined in a way that serves to highlight the human drama and emphasize the sense of the frontier age coming to a close. Shame Ford otherwise made "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" miserable for everyone involved, though.

A revisionist Western everybody should watch at least once, "High Noon" tells the story of Gary Cooper's Marshal Will Kane, who's preparing to leave the frontier town of Hadleyville, New Mexico, with his new bride, Amy (Grace Kelly). When he learns that his former nemesis Frank Miller is on the loose and is headed for Hadleyville, Kane decides to stay and prepare for a confrontation. But this is not your typical Western hero. In fact, rather than facing down his outlaw enemies with the steely resolve of a classic Western gunfighter, he spends most of "High Noon" asking people for help. No such help is forthcoming, and Kane is forced into the final confrontation alone.

Howard Hawks and John Wayne made "Rio Bravo" out of hatred for "High Noon," perhaps predictably given the Duke would never dream of playing a man who gave the impression he needed help of any sort. But the film is considered one of the great Westerns — and all it took was one small town to create a masterpiece of tension and psychological drama.

More importantly, in director Fred Zinnemann's estimation, the town itself was crucial to the story being told. As he put it in his biography, "A Life in the Movies," (via Turner Classic Movies), "[Kane's] town – symbol of a democracy gone soft – faces a horrendous threat to its people's way of life." "High Noon" was about apathy and the loss of a collective belief in standing up for what's right. Like in so many Westerns before and after, then, the town at the center of "High Noon" functioned as a microcosm of society as a whole, and was all Zinnemann and co. needed to tell their story.

Don Siegel's "The Shootist" bowed in 1976, at a time when the era of John Wayne was coming to a close in more ways than one. In a literal sense, the Duke only lasted three more years after the release of this film before he passed away from stomach cancer. In a figurative sense, the traditional big screen Western epitomized by Wayne was, at best, fading. More accurately, it had already been superseded by the revisionist Westerns of directors such as Sam Peckinpah and the man whom Wayne never liked to admit represented his successor, Clint Eastwood.

This story of an aging gunfighter learning he has terminal cancer plays out entirely in Carson City, Nevada. Here, Wayne's John Bernard "J. B." Books arrives and rents a room with Lauren Bacall's Bond Rogers and her son, Gillom Rogers (Ron Howard). Not wanting to die a slow, painful death as a result of his disease, Books arranges to meet three dangerous crack shots at a saloon, and is ultimately felled by a bartender's bullet. The final scene sees Gillom Rogers return the favor, shooting the bartender before tossing Books' gun and seemingly rejecting the notion of following in the footsteps of Wayne's shootist.

This entire story takes place within Carson City, where Books decides to spend his final days as both he and the Old West itself fade. "The Shootist" was Wayne's final film, and while many surely wished he went out with some sort of grandiose ode to both the country that birthed the Western and the genre that made him a star, this comparatively modest swan song, contained within the confines of Carson City, proved to be the perfect farewell.

#3590. Sydney Sweeney’s Extremely R-Rated 131-Minute Thriller Is Officially Streaming on HBO

Perfect for those who love an outrageous twist

Despite its overwhelming commercial success, Freida McFadden’s psychological thriller, The Housemaid, is far from a perfect read. Trope-heavy and full of obvious contrivances, The Housemaid sets up a tense domestic thriller premise that is meant to be consumed as a fast-paced popcorn novel. This, however, sets the stage for a pulpy screen adaptation, one that mimics the conventions of a lurid thriller with some decent character writing to round things out.

Bridesmaids director Paul Feig’s The Housemaid lives up to these expectations. Formulaic but utterly entertaining, the film features Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried as characters that seem to be pitted against each other. The Housemaid is a great fit for anyone who likes erotic thrillers of the Verity variety, wherein the plot features some sort of unexpected twist to keep things interesting. If you’ve been meaning to watch The Housemaid from the comfort of your home, the film is available to stream on HBO Max right now.

Recently paroled Millie (Sweeney) tries to put her past behind her by working as a live-in maid for Nina (Seyfried), who lives with her husband, Andrew (Brandon Sklenar), and daughter, Cece (Indiana Elle). Nina needs help because she is pregnant, and Millie needs to maintain a lawful employment status, making the arrangement feasible at first. Nina’s suburban mansion in Great Neck, Long Island, is opulent to the point of appearing gaudy, giving Millie all the more reason to commit to the job seriously.

Unfortunately, things start to feel off after some time. Millie is asked to stay in an attic bedroom that locks from the outside, and Nina starts making veiled threats, asking Millie to stay away from her husband. Things escalate quickly, going from mild accusations to full-blown breakdowns that make Millie feel horribly trapped inside a ridiculously spacious mansion.

The Housemaid toys with our expectations as it builds its suspense, allowing us to immerse ourselves in the minute details of Nina and Millie’s frayed dynamic. Is Nina truly troubled like everyone wants us to believe, or is there a grander conspiracy at play here? Although Nina’s erratic behavior is a cause for genuine concern, Millie and Andrew are drawn closer amid this chaos, leading to the start of a complicated relationship that might change everything we know about these characters.

Unlike the source material, The Housemaid takes itself a bit too seriously. That, however, doesn’t get in the way of the curveballs that Feig throws at us after the shocking midway twist is revealed. Most pulpy thrillers thrive on this formula, including The Voyeurs, which is yet another engaging movies starring Sweeney. The Housemaid makes good use of this tonal shift, allowing characters like Nina to unravel more layers of her complex, inconsistent behavior.

Even before the film hones in on the truth, The Housemaid is smart enough to keep us guessing. Nina’s behavior (which often encroaches on horror movie territory) is backed up by whispers from her high-society friends and anecdotes from other house staff. Andrew’s perspective is also crucial here. He comes across as a doting husband and father, heartbroken that his wife is no longer the person he fell in love with. Millie’s escalating attraction to Andrew fuels these confusing rumors, but we’re often given glimpses of a truth we’re not yet privy to.

What The Housemaid does accomplish is a sense of dramatic climax that is significantly toned down in the book. “There’s things that work in the book that are really satisfying, but on the big screen you always want more," Feig told The Hollywood Reporter to explain his need to up the ante. Feig also uses perspective shifts to tie disparate clues together, and Seyfried’s standout performance contains subtle hints for eagle-eyed audiences to decipher. Things turn sleazy when they need to, without diving into the pure camp of genre entries like Body Double (1984) or Wild Things (1998).

If you like entertaining psychological thrillers with a pulpy edge, The Housemaid is a solid choice. This is no Gone Girl, but taut atmosphere and pacing make this movie feel more than serviceable.

#3588. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3587. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Of 1995, Ranked

1995 was a big year for movies. "Toy Story" launched one of cinema's most reliable hit-makers in Pixar and helped redefine what animation could be. One of the greatest crime thrillers of all time came our way with "Seven." Michael Mann's crowning achievement "Heat" was gifted to action lovers around the world. Nicolas Cage delivered his Oscar-winning performance in "Leaving Las Vegas." But it was also one heck of a year for science fiction.

In terms of historical context, Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" revolutionized Hollywood just two years earlier with its blend of CGI and practical effects, with the industry rapidly adopting computer generated visuals (not always with great results). Meanwhile, other movies were still relying heavily on practical effects, which gives movies from this era a specific feeling. It was a unique time for science fiction, a genre that's often been at the forefront of adoption for new technology in cinema while serving as a breeding ground for underrated gems.

We're going to take a look at the best of the best that sci-fi had to offer viewers in 1995. From groundbreaking anime to rubber suit monster movie goodness and everything in between, there's a little something for everyone here. Let's dig in.

I can't sit here and rightfully say that "Species" is A-class cinema. I can't say that it's the best that the science fiction genre had to offer in the year of our lord 1995. What I can say is that, more than 30 years removed, it's a delightful relic of its time, one that is sexy, ridiculous, and a great deal of fun. Sci-fi doesn't always have to be serious to be seriously enjoyable.

Directed by Roger Donaldson, the film centers on Xavier Fitch (Ben Kingsley) who intercepts a space transmission containing the genetic sequence for an alien life form. He uses it to produce "Sil" (Natasha Henstridge), a gorgeous alien-human hybrid. Fitch's team is concerned by her rapid rate of growth before Sil destroys the laboratory and begins a violent quest for a male human to impregnate her. The U.S. government dispatches top assassin Preston Lennox (Michael Madsen) and a team of experts to stop her.

"Species" is a wacky movie that features some incredible makeup effects and not-so-great CGI. It has Oscar-caliber actors like Sir. Ben Kingsley giving his best to a bonkers script, while guys like Michael Madsen gladly ham it up. It was also a breakout role for the movie's lead, Natasha Henstridge, who has a true scene-stealing presence about her. She is undoubtedly the main reason why this movie sticks out in so many people's minds all these years later.

This also spawned a franchise, with the "Species" sequels bringing DND and T&A to the DTV market. I can't in good conscience recommend those midnight movie sequels to the masses, but I can easily defend the original as a worthwhile bit of '90s sci-fi goodness. (Ryan Scott)

The "Gamera" movies are many things. The original entries are campier kaiju classics oft-remembered as corny fuel for some of the best episodes of "Mystery Science Theater 3000." But the franchise has also produced some genuinely excellent entries in the genre. Case in point: "Gamera: Guardian of the Universe." Directed by Shūsuke Kaneko, this launched a whole new era for the classic Japanese monster, with this particular entry serving as an excellent launching pad for Gamera's grand return.

In this "Gamera" cinematic adventure, a ship runs aground on a mysterious atoll leading to an investigation by insurance representative Kusanagi (Akira Onodera). He discovers an ancient bead that he gives to his daughter Asagi (Ayako Fujitani). Meanwhile, ornithologist Nagamine (Shinobu Nakayama) investigates reports of a new species of large bird named Gyaos. As the Gyaos begin to attack, an ancient guardian with a bond to Asagi emerges.

By the mid-'90s, so much of Hollywood was already relying heavily on CGI to create special effects. Part of what's great about "Guardian of the Universe" is that it still has that tangible, rubber suit monster magic. Yet, technology had gotten better since the '60s and '70s, allowing for those practical effects to shine even brighter. The result? Some of the best practical kaiju action one could ever hope to find.

This film redefined what a "Gamera" movie could be. No longer was this just the lesser-than, turtle-like cousin to "Godzilla." Gamera was undeniably cool now. As was Gyaos, an impeccably designed addition to the franchise. It also served as a springboard for several sequels, including "Gamera 3: Revenge of Iris," one of the best sci-fi movies of 1999. It was a damn fine time for monster movies. (Ryan Scott)

There are dozens of "Godzilla" movies of varying quality dating back to 1954 when the King of the Monsters first debuted on the big screen. But for those who have a fondness for a time when the one they call Gojira was still a rubber suited monster duking it out with other monsters made of rubber, it's hard to do better than "Godzilla vs. Destroyah." Directed by Takao Okawara, it's one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time.

The film wastes no time as it opens with a burning Godzilla, on the verge of meltdown that could threaten all of humanity, emerging to lay siege to Hong Kong. Meanwhile, horrifying new organisms are discovered in Japan and these crustacean-like creatures are seemingly born of the Oxygen Destroyer, the weapon that killed the original Godzilla. These separate monster problems ultimately lead us to a kaiju clash for the ages.

This is the final entry in the so-called Heisi era of the "Godzilla" franchise, which has by far the best practical monsters in the 70-plus year history of the series. One would be hard-pressed to find more impressive monster designs than that of Destroyah, a hulking, terrifying, hellish vision that is worth the price of admission alone. Plus, the design of the burning Godzilla is unique and metal AF.

With lots of sci-fi craziness, just enough cheese, and some of the best practical kaiju action ever put on the silver screen, this is a must-see for monster movie lovers. Not for nothing, it's the only "Godzilla" movie that currently boasts a perfect critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. It deserves it, in my humble opinion. (Ryan Scott)

A time-travel movie, a post-apocalyptic movie, and all-around a mind-melting piece of sci-fi, "12 Monkeys" is a wild ride. Arguably Terry Gilliam's best film, it loosely adapts Chris Marker's 1962 experimental short film "La Jetée," and follows Bruce Willis as James Cole, a convict sent back in time to find out information about a man-made virus that wiped out most of humanity back in his time. What starts as a relatively simple mission devolves into an exploration of madness, time, and dreams, set in a world that is slowly coming apart. Though made in 1995, the film's focus on how we perceive information and decipher the truth among all the noise is as relevant today as it's ever been. This is not a feel-good movie, but rather a story of rebellion and resilience in a world that tries to tear you apart for perceiving things differently, and Gilliam adequately captures that thought with a cold and dark film that reflects the slow descent into madness of its protagonist.

Even if there's little hope to be found by the end of the movie, "12 Monkeys" is still thrilling and hugely entertaining. It walks the line between commerciality and art, with Gilliam employing two of the biggest stars in Hollywood at the time (Willis and Brad Pitt), while also presenting them without an ounce of vanity. It's a big production, but it sneaks in a provocative and idiosyncratic story with a bleak vision of the future. It also has a layered story that never compromises its singular vision. (Rafael Motamayor)

There are few sci-fi films as generation-defining as Mamoru Oshii's adaptation of Masamune Shirow's "Ghost in the Shell." This is a film that's inspired countless filmmakers around the globe, in both animation and live-action. We wouldn't have "The Matrix" if it wasn't for "Ghost in the Shell," and titans like James Cameron and Steven Spielberg count themselves among its many fans. Plus, it's just genuinely a thrilling and monumental piece of science-fiction cinema. The film is set in the then-distant future, at a time when most people have some sort of cybernetic implant and some even have cyber brains that allow access to the internet. The story follows a cyborg public security agent hunting down an enigmatic hacker.

Mamoru Oshii does a great job of condensing the complex and dense plotting of the original manga, while adding his own take on the material. This is a dark film with austere seriousness that meditates on the nature of self, identity, and our relationship with technology. It can take several viewings to fully grasp the many thematic layers present in this film and the way each scene builds on some thematic idea, adding to the main character's crisis of identity as she contemplates how much of her humanity is left under all her cybernetic implants. "Ghost in the Shell" is also a straight-up beautiful movie to look at, with Production I.G delivering a stunning combination of traditional cel animation with CGI animation. In many ways, this is the '90s answer to "Akira" in how the film pushes forward what animation can do, with lens effects and attention to light and shadow serving to make a film that looks like nothing before or since. (Rafael Motamayor)

As soon as the news came out that there would be a movie about the making of Rocky, I was pumped! The timing truly is perfect, as this great sports film is celebrating its 50th anniversary this year. So, Rocky fans are sure to raise their fists in the air as they head to theaters. However, Ryan Gosling has already done that. Yes, that's right, Ryan Gosling gave I Play Rocky his stamp of approval, which is making me put this movie high on my watchlist.

Early reviews of I Play Rocky were great. With its star, Anthony Ippolito, nailing Sylvester Stallone’s voice and swagger, I felt like it would be easy to love this upcoming flick. However, it just got easier, because while AnnaSophia Robb (who plays Sylvester Stallone's wife, Sasha) was on The Today Show, she spoke about none other than Ryan Gosling giving the cast his stamp of approval:

It was wild. I have never experienced anything like that. We’re at CinemaCon and we’re doing, you know, press. It’s absolute chaos. And all of a sudden, there’s this kerfuffle and I turn around and Ryan Gosling is there. And he goes, ‘Is this the I Play Rocky cast? I love the movie! It was terrific!’

Wow! Given what a talented actor Ryan Gosling is, it has to be such an honor to receive a compliment from him. Just as I was already excited for the drama, The Notebook actor hyped me up even more.

I would assume that no matter how accomplished or famous you are, to have someone you look up to compliment your work must mean the world. That was certainly the case for the cast of I Play Rocky during this interaction with the Project Hail Mary star, as Robb continued:

And I was gobsmacked. My jaw was on the floor and it was just, it meant so much because I had just watched him in Project Hail Mary and I loved it. And just to have somebody you’ve been watching your whole life love the film. It just, it meant the world. And we’re all sitting there like, wow.

Yes, it’s very easy to be a Ryan Gosling fan when you watch his best romances and top underrated movies. So, I can only imagine how overwhelming it must have been to be on the receiving end of his compliment. It’s clear the La La Land actor knows a good movie when he sees it and isn’t afraid to give acclaim to it. (Plus it doesn't hurt that his latest movie, Project Hail Mary, features some very notable Rocky references.)

As I Play Rocky makes its way to theaters, I'm happy we now know that Ryan Gosling gave it his stamp of approval. I’m sure he won’t be the only one once we all get to see talented actors shape the story of how the masterpiece of Rocky was made. You all have the chance to feel what Gosling is feeling as the 2026 movie release is playing in select theaters now.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3585. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3584. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3583. The Best King Ghidorah Movie To Watch After Godzilla Minus Zero Is Streaming On HBO Max

"Godzilla Minus Zero" may not be as good as its immediate predecessor, but Takashi Yamazaki brings some truly spectacular kaiju action to the big screen in his "Godzilla Minus One" sequel. The film has a sense of scope and scale that we haven't really seen in the 70-year-old franchise, with impeccable VFX that capture the sheer destruction of the giant monsters that battle it out in the movie. Yamazaki also captures the true horrors of what a kaiju attack would look like, putting the film's R-rating to good use with some gruesome imagery.

The highlight of the movie is, surprisingly enough, not Godzilla. Instead, it's the golden, armless dragon with three heads and two tails known as Ghidorah. "Godzilla Minus Zero" retains Ghidorah's alien origin while reimagining him as a translucent blob that absorbs creatures and adopts their traits, allowing him to evolve into a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning and can make things float.

Though Ghidorah's design unfortunately leaked before the film's release, he still looks absolutely perfect. More so, the character brings some silliness to Yamazaki's take on the Godzilla universe, as the inclusion of aliens means future sequels can now bring in anything from Mechagodzilla to even Gigan. And yet, Ghidorah remains scary and awe-inspiring. It's easy to see why he's been Godzilla's main archenemy for decades and is the one kaiju that, at least in the eyes of the public, presents a real threat to the king of the monsters.

Unfortunately, despite him showing up in over a dozen movies, most of Ghidorah's film appearances aren't that great. Luckily, the best Ghidorah movie, by far, is currently streaming on HBO Max — namely, the king of terror's debut in the appropriately titled 1964 film "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster."

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was released back in 1964 as the fifth film in the Godzilla franchise, bringing together Godzilla, Mothra, and Rodan, who must all team up to take down the titular Ghidorah (lest the kaiju cause humanity to perish).

This is not only one of the best Godzilla movies of all time, it's also a hugely important film in the long-running franchise. That's because the movie marked a change in the king of monsters, introducing the idea of Godzilla as humankind's savior rather than just a destructive force. Up until that point, Godzilla would either attack human cities or battle other kaiju, but the latter scenario tended to center around some kind of territorial dispute or petty grievance. In other words, Godzilla would act more like a grumpy old man trying to keep kids off his lawn than a hero.

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," however, fully transformed Godzilla into a force for good that would team up with other monsters in an effort to defend the people of Earth. Indeed, for decades after that, the king of the monsters would mostly help defend humans against other threats, taking on the likes of MechaGodzilla, Biollante, and plenty of other kaijus.

On top of that, "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" is just plain fun as a movie. Director Ishirō Honda finds a great balance between the serious tone of his original 1954 "Godzilla" (which focuses on the horror that surrounds the kaiju) and the campiness that would become a staple of the "Godzilla" franchise in the coming years. It's a rather ambitious film, too, with four monsters sharing the screen, yet it never feels too busy or disjointed.

Though Godzilla has fought plenty of villains over the last 70 years, none have managed to leave a lasting impact the way King Ghidorah has. When he was first introduced, kaiju were either all bad or portrayed as animals we should root against. But Ghidorah was the first proper villain of the "Godzilla" franchise, and he is treated as such. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" takes its time teasing the arrival of the titular dragon, building dread and making sure you understand Ghidorah is a big enough threat that Godzilla would actually join forces with other kaiju to take him down.

It's why 2019's rather underrated "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" borrows so much from "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," pairing Godzilla with the same allies he has in the 1964 film in order to square off with the more powerful Ghidorah. That movie understands that a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning is already a pretty imposing image and the perfect way to make Godzilla appear heroic.

Now, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has continued that tradition, turning King Ghidorah into a terrifying monster. This new movie isn't in a hurry to bring Godzilla back, and in the meantime, we watch as Ghidorah lays waste to Japan, causing harrowing devastation with his terrific powers (including the ability to make buildings levitate, which he uses to kill a whole bunch of people by dropping them to their painful deaths). The film also introduces the idea of Ghidorah constantly evolving, with his design changing throughout the movie as he grows heads, turns golden, and ultimately gains Godzilla-like dorsal plates, along with the king of the monsters' ability to wield atomic breath.

Ghidorah will always be Godzilla's greatest foe, and you can watch his first and best appearance on HBO Max.

Since Jodie Sweetin and Andrea Barber launched their Full House rewatch podcast, How Rude, Tanneritos!, plenty of BTS sitcom tea has been spilled. From the fact that producers had a preferred Olsen twin to work with to the anger on set when Candace Cameron Bure cut her hair without warning, there's been so much to learn about the TGIF show. And, on the latest podcast episode, it was revealed that one actor had “too big a pack” to be wearing biker shorts for a scene with Kimmy Gibbler, and this sounds so cringey.

In the season 7 episode of “Love on the Rocks,” DJ Tanner debates whether or not to break up with her boyfriend, Steve Hale. When she goes mountain climbing with Kimmy and her boyfriend, Keanu, she gains a new perspective on her life and relationship. While discussing the episode, in a recent episode of How Rude, Tanneritos!, Kimmy actress Andrea Barber exposed a rather revealing detail about her on-screen boyfriend that cropped up amid filming:

This poor actor, Keanu. So originally, he wasn’t wearing his jacket and it was just his shirt and his biker shorts. But, the bike shorts were a little tight. And a little too revealing.

Yes, poor actor! When you rewatch the episode, the biker shorts Keanu was wearing really did look tight, almost like spandex. And for a family-friendly show, it makes sense to cover that up. Like Sweetin humorously said, that’s just too much information for families at home to see.

It’s common for wardrobe changes to happen when an actor on a family-friendly sitcom is showing a little growth down there. That happened to Jaleel White when he was asked to hide his bulge in Family Matters. In the case of Brian Evans, who played Keanu, Barber explained that the wardrobe department had other ideas to hide that area:

They got a note. Costumes got a note from Video Village. And so, they had to quickly find this jacket. A long jacket to cover.

Well, I’ve got to say, the long jacket worked. You can’t see anything. Hey, you do what you have to do to keep the Full House episode G-rated.

Anyone curious as to how Brian Evans felt about the embarrassing wardrobe change should know he told EW that he “didn’t know what was happening.” Not only that, but he also revealed the priceless reaction his mother had when one of the crew members told him he had “too big of a pack" for a teenager on this show”:

I remember seeing my mother’s face sitting at the studio audience just beet red, laughing.

This certainly isn't the kind of moment I would've expected to hear regarding the long-binge-watchable show, but it's also a funny piece of information. Thank goodness the costume department of the ABC sitcom was right on top of it. Otherwise, I could imagine the producers receiving some not-so-flattering letters from parents.

It’ll be hard not to think about this little (or not-so-little) tidbit of information when watching this Full House episode moving forward. Still, the detail shouldn't be too distracting for audiences given how the jacket comes into play. Fans can watch “Love on the Rocks” and more episodes of the show by streaming them with either a Hulu subscription or a Disney+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3581. Anya Taylor-Joy's Billion-Dollar Sci-Fi Epic Officially Sets New Streaming Home on Netflix

Illumination's greatest achievement this year takes full advantage of Taylor-Joy's talents

Anya Taylor-Joy captivated audiences as chess prodigy Beth Harmon in Netflix’s 2020 miniseries The Queen’s Gambit. Her performance balanced poise with emotional depth, creating a character whose story and presence have lingered with viewers long after the series ended. Even years later, the role remains especially memorable — more so than her appearances in action-packed franchises, including Fox’s Marvel superhero film The New Mutants.

Though Taylor-Joy’s remarkable range and phenomenal acting have earned widespread admiration, one role in particular won the hearts of families everywhere. This sci-fi film revealed a fresh comedic side of her talent, adding another dimension to her on-screen performances. It also became one of the greatest animated achievements of all time, the second-highest-grossing animated film of 2026.

What film could we possibly be talking about? The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, of course. And it's coming to Netflix later this month on Nov. 30.

Directed by the creative minds behind Teen Titans Go! (Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic), The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is a thrilling action-comedy based on Nintendo's Mario video game franchise (created by Shigeru Miyamoto) and produced by Illumination and Nintendo.

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie also serves as the sequel to the original 2023 film, which followed Mario (Chris Pratt) and Luigi (Charlie Day) on their first arrival in the Mushroom Kingdom. This time, though, the Mario brothers embark on a galaxy-spanning adventure. Set some time after their victory over Bowser (Jack Black), whom they’ve shrunk and are trying to rehabilitate, Mario and Luigi are enjoying life as the Mushroom Kingdom’s saviors.

But things take a turn for the worse when they discover that Princess Rosalina (Brie Larson) has been kidnapped by Bowser Jr. (Benny Safdie). As it turns out, Bowser Jr. is still pretty steamed because Mario and Luigi beat his father and shrank him down to run around in a cage like a particularly thorny hamster.

The downside is that Bowser Jr. hasn’t just tossed Rosalina into a castle down the road for Mario and Luigi to rescue. Bowser Jr. has taken Rosalina somewhere much harder to reach: a vast, nearly empty region of the universe known as space.

Fortunately, they have a whole lot of luck on their side. (And a new ally in Yoshi, voiced by Donald Glover.) Together, they face the challenge of getting Rosalina back. Will they succeed? Watch and find out for yourselves.

One of the most exciting things about this action-packed sequel is that several stars return to reprise their roles, including Taylor-Joy as Princess Peach.

Below is the full cast of The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is widely considered a success. In June this year, it crossed a major milestone, grossing more than $1 billion at the global box office. Sure, it isn’t quite as successful as its predecessor film, The Super Mario Bros. Movie, but an animated movie raking in over a billion dollars is nothing to turn your nose up at.

Though it did well commercially, critics weren’t as enamored with Illumination’s second outing in the Mario universe. Peter Bradshaw of The Guardian gave The Super Mario Galaxy Movie one out of five stars, and likened it to a “bland screensaver of a movie that's actually worse than AI”, whereas Clarisse Loughrey of The Independent scored the film two out of five, calling it "a joke-free sequel that doubles down on its own blandness."

Polygon’s own review was much more favorable, with reviewer Michael McWhertor praising the film for taking “some welcome swings at diverse animation styles.”

Still, if you’re expecting emotional or mature depth from The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, it may not be the film for you.

Given how commercially successful The Super Mario Galaxy Movie was, and that Nintendo has 45 years of Mario content to draw from, we would be more surprised if a sequel wasn’t in the works.

The movie’s post-credit scene also revealed yet another beloved Nintendo character, just as The Super Mario Bros. Movie did. If Nintendo doesn’t expand on that, we’ll eat our hats.

The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is currently streaming on Peacock and arrives on Netflix on Nov. 30.

#3580. Marvel's 2027 Release Schedule: All 8 Movies And TV Shows Explained

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While there is only one Marvel Cinematic Universe movie premiering in 2027, if the production goes as planned, there are plenty of Marvel projects debuting throughout the year. Whether they're a part of the MCU or other titles based on Marvel's countless comic book properties, there is enough to keep fans excited. These range from returning animated shows and miniseries to eagerly anticipated live-action projects on television and the big screen. We're gathering them all here together so you can keep track of each of them in one convenient place.

From announced release dates and cast members to the details that we know so far, each of these projects offer tantalizing directions for Marvel's superheroes and supervillains. We're also including projects that aren't produced directly by Marvel Studios, some of which are no less exciting. As with all release dates in television and film, the premiere dates mentioned here are subject to change.

With that in mind, here is Marvel's 2027 release schedule with all eight movies and TV shows explained.

When it debuted in 2025, the Disney+ animated series "Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" breathed new life into fan-favorite webslinger. Set in its own universe, the show has Peter Parker (Hudson Thames) receive a well-connected mentor in Norman Osborn (Colman Domingo) as he starts his superhero career. The show takes its cues from the MCU, with guest heroes and villains appearing semi-regularly, but visually, it's inspired by the artwork of Steve Ditko and John Romita, Jr. Through it all, the series maintains sight on how Peter's double life takes a toll on his high school life and the importance of having a good mentor figure.

"Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" set up Season 2 with Norman obtaining a piece of the symbiote that gave Peter his powers in this universe. This hints at the inclusion of Venom, with Josh Keaton cast as Eddie Brock, a fun nod after Keaton played Peter in "The Spectacular Spider-Man." Peter's long-lost father Richard Parker, revealed to be incarcerated, was also silently introduced at the end of the season, setting up an uncomfortable family reunion. With Gwen Stacy also joining the show, "Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" is set to go deeper into the superhero mythos when it returns on January 13, 2027.

It feels like just yesterday that Charlie Cox made his big return to reclaim the mantle of Daredevil, after Netflix canceled the original version of the superhero series in 2018. Fast-forward nearly a decade later and we're preparing for the third and final season of the Disney+ revival series "Daredevil: Born Again." The second season finale set up Season 3 with Matt Murdock (Cox) revealing his superhero secret to the world, resulting in his incarceration for his violent vigilantism. Just as Season 2 saw Jessica Jones (Krysten Ritter) and Luke Cage (Mike Colter) return, Season 3 will bring back Danny Rand (Finn Jones) and Elektra Natchios (Élodie Yung).

Though "Daredevil: Born Again" was canceled by Marvel months before its Season 3 premiere, we're still looking forward to it. The series remains as intense and brutal as it ever was on Netflix while incorporating more nods to the wider MCU around it. Plus, this could be the last time that we see Daredevil and the Defenders back in action again, at least with the familiar Netflix era actors in their roles. Sure to put Matt Murdock and his friends through the wringer, "Daredevil: Born Again" Season 3 will hopefully continue to not pull its punches. It's expected to premiere in March 2027.

The acclaimed animated movie "Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse" ended on a cliffhanger that left audiences hanging back in 2023. After delays surrounding "Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse" pushed back the sequel's intended release date by several years, it looks on track for a June 18, 2027 premiere. The movie will answer what happens to teenager superhero Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) after he was stranded in an alternate universe with a more brutal doppelganger to contend with. The preceding movie's co-director Justin K. Thompson reunites with "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse" co-director Bob Persichetti for the sequel.

At the time of this writing, Sony hasn't so much as released an official teaser trailer for "Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse." This restrained promotional approach has served the studio well before, specifically with the gangbusters reception to this year's "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." We're certainly at the edge of our seats to see if the creative team can stick the landing and, two movies in, they haven't let us down so far. The "Spider-Verse" movies are ranked highly among the best Spider-Man movies ever so, going "Beyond the Spider-Verse" should be worth the wait.

Fans had to wait just over two years for "X-Men '97" Season 2, but that gap reportedly won't happen with Season 3. A continuation of the beloved "X-Men: Animated Series," what some would consider the definitive versions of the characters, the mutant superheroes were left reeling coming out of Season 2. The villainous Apocalypse (Ross Marquand) was defeated, but the X-Men had lost several of their own, most notably Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough). Meanwhile, mutantkind's relationship with humanity is more fraught than ever while Mystique (Randall Carpenter) has her own fiendish plans.

"X-Men '97" Season 2 was a dazzling return for the hit revival series, and Season 3 looks to tighten its narrative focus by comparison. One of the weak points of the second season was dividing its narrative across three separate timelines for the first half of the season. Based on how Season 2 ended, Season 3 will likely unfold entirely from a single timeline, as its characters face new threats. A more sophisticated storytelling approach to its classic preceding series, "X-Men '97" has fans of the show revisit these enduring characters without treading too heavily on pure nostalgia.

We were pleasantly surprised how dark and intense "Marvel Zombies" got compared to the rest of Marvel's recent animated output, bringing a horrific edge to an alternate MCU. The series is set to get a line of two-part specials set in its world, each focused on a different character in its world overrun by ravenous undead. After "Marvel Zombies" cut the Winter Soldier from its first season's story, the character will headline the first of these specials. The show is set to be directed by Bryan Andrews, who directed the main series, with its episodes expected to debut on Disney+ in October.

Given the ending of "Marvel Zombies," it's unclear if Bucky Barnes' story will take place before, during, or after the main series. "Marvel Zombies: The Winter Soldier" will be followed by a 2028 special "The Fist of Khonshu" and 2029 special "The Last Guardian." These specials are poised to expand the terror-fueled scope of the main series while depicting how different characters react to the zombie apocalypse. With his particular set of skills, Bucky is about to be put to the test in "Marvel Zombies: The Winter Soldier" and we'll be there to watch in October 2027.

With "Avengers: Secret Wars" reportedly moving its production into 2027, a delayed release date may be in the cards for the MCU movie. But, at least at the time of this writing, the upcoming film is still officially scheduled for a wide theatrical release on December 17, 2027. As the sequel to "Avengers: Doomsday," details about "Secret Wars" are currently being kept tightly under wraps until "Doomsday" debuts. This extends to the movie's cast list, though Samuel L. Jackson has claimed that his next Marvel movie as Nick Fury will be the 2027 release.

While plot details remain unconfirmed, the movie is expected to adapt the 2015 comic book series "Secret Wars" by Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribic. This storyline saw Doctor Doom rule over a composite reality formed by the remnants of the multiverse with the heroes banding together to overthrow him. Hickman himself is a consultant on "Secret Wars," so the movie may follow its comic book source material more faithfully than anticipated. Regardless, we're excited to see where the MCU goes next after the cataclysmic turn of events that's sure to unfold in "Doomsday."

After a 35-episode single season, "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends" came to an end in April 2026. This paves the wave for another early-age animated series, "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends," which is set to premiere sometime in 2027. Like "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends," this series features versions of its popular superheroes as children working together and enjoying their friendship. Though the voice cast hasn't been announced, it's set to include Spider-Man, Captain America, Iron Man, Black Panther, Black Widow, Thor, Ms. Marvel, and Hulk.

No official release window for "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends" has been announced so far, bu, if it matches "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends," it should be in the summer. It's also unknown how many episodes the show's first season will receive. But the series will air on Disney Jr. and likely be available to stream on Disney+ afterwards. A good primer for younger audiences into the Marvel Universe, "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends" is an inviting tour of its superhero-filled world.

For viewers who may be too young for the "Spider-Verse" movies, the animated series "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" has got them covered. The early age-friendly show premiered in 2021 and is set to release its sixth season on Disney Jr. in 2027 before coming to Disney+. Like the "Spider-Verse" movies, the show revolves around Peter Parker (Nick A. Fisher), Miles Morales (Carter Young), and Gwen Stacy (Audrey Bennett). Like "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends," the show features grade school iterations of the superhero characters as they get into super-powered hijinks and celebrate their friendship.

No official release window has currently been announced for "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" Season 6, but historically, the show has released new episodes during the summer. The series features the trio facing all the usual supervillains in Spider-Man's rogues' gallery but with the action and stakes far less intense. It's unknown which new characters are joining the show in Season 6, but Season 5 added Silk (Aveline Choi) to the heroic ensemble. Bringing freewheeling and fun set of adventures starring younger webslingers, "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" is a great gateway into the world of Spider-Man.

#3578. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

What do you think of the new Health app in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

There’s a lot of love about Season 1 of Prime Video’s popular hockey romance Off Campus. The book-to-screen adaptation has incredible chemistry, love triangles, shirtless hockey guys, and even a live performance from indie pop-rock star Remi Wolf. I’ve been spamming her music ever since the show came out, including her new album Mud. Her raspy belt is incredibly unique, and I only just found out that it actually got her pretty far on American Idol.

I’ve actually been a fan of Remi Wolf for a few years now, so I was pleasantly surprised when I started watching Off Campus, and she popped up as herself on stage in Season 1, Episode 1, which is available to stream with an Amazon Prime subscription. However, I had no idea this wasn’t her first TV appearance. Wolf was actually first introduced to audiences on Season 13 of American Idol, and recently reminisced with People about her experience on the iconic singing competition:

I got pretty decently far, and it was a cool experience to see how the entertainment industry works because I had no experience whatsoever in that world.

Wolf, who at the time was 17 years old, made it decently far in the competition after auditioning “on a whim.” She wowed judges Harry Connick Jr., Jennifer Lopez, and Keith Urban to make it to Hollywood Week before getting cut from the competition. However, the “Bottle” singer said she was grateful her time on Idol ended there:

I was such a baby, and I’m so glad that I was able to carve my own path as a baby growing into an adult rather than having that early influence on me by executives and stuff. I feel like my frontal cortex was not developed enough to handle it.

One thing I love about Remi Wolf’s music is that it’s her own unique sound, and I love that she has built her career off living completely true to herself, and that Island Records, the label she is signed to, has allowed and encouraged her to do that. I have to wonder if teenage Remi Wolf in 2014 could have predicted that her run on Idol, and eventual exit, would have led to a cameo on one of Prime Video’s most acclaimed shows of 2026.

Wolf first gained fame from her hit single “Photo I.D.” in 2021, and has since released three studio albums. Her performance in Off Campus features some of her biggest songs off her second studio album Big Ideas, including "Soup", "Toro", and "Alone In Miami."

Her latest album Mud was released on October 9 of this year, with the 30-year-old describing the project on her Instagram as “my favorite, my healer, my family, my precious, my blood, sweat, and tears.” It’s clearly her most vulnerable project to date, prompted by her decision a year and a half ago to become sober.

I would love to see Remi Wolf return to Off Campus in Season 2, which has officially been confirmed to drop on Prime April 28, 2027. The “Sexy Villain” singer said on the Zach Sang Show that she would be down to return, but that she has no idea where they would work her into the story, and I have to agree. However, I would love to hear some of her new songs off Mud included in the soundtrack when Season 2 premieres.
