#3550. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3549. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3548. Sarah Michelle Gellar Passed On A Martin Scorsese Movie Because Of Buffy The Vampire Slayer

Martin Scorsese's filmography is filled with films that took decades to get off the ground. By the 21st Century, Scorsese had settled into a statesman of cinema stature, and (to the joy of cinephiles everywhere) he's cashed in decades of chits and clout to deliver passion projects like 2016's "Silence," 2019's "The Irishman," and 2002's "Gangs of New York."

The latter draws on a 1928 nonfiction book, "The Gangs of New York" by Herbert Ashbury, that tracked the history of New York's organized crime from the 19th to 20th Century. As the book and movie show, that tale is intertwined with how Irish and Italian immigrants settled in New York went from spat-upon outsiders to true Americans.

Scorsese read "The Gangs of New York" in 1970 and acquired the rights to make a movie out of it in 1979, but development took over 20 years. It's no surprise that in that time, Scorsese's plans for "Gangs of New York" evolved. The final film — set mostly in the 1860s — is an epic revenge narrative starring Leonardo DiCaprio as the fictional Amsterdam Vallon and Daniel Day-Lewis as a fictionalized version of real New York gang leader Bill the Butcher (named William Cutting in the film, but William Poole in real life).

One change close to the finish line was the casting of female lead Jenny, Amsterdam's love interest and a thief in Bill's organization. Sarah Michelle Gellar, a star thanks to her role on the then contemporary TV series "Buffy the Vampire Slayer," was considered for the part. However, her commitments to "Buffy" (which was in its fifth season when "Gangs of New York" shot from December 2000 to March 2001) meant she couldn't sign on. Jenny went on to be played by Cameron Diaz instead.

Now, Cameron Diaz wasn't Martin Scorsese's first choice understudy for Jenny. He was also interested in casting Sarah Polley, but now-disgraced producer Harvey Weinstein insisted on a bigger name. (Weinstein was the reason Scorsese made sure the film debuted as his director's cut, too.) So, Diaz, a comedy starlet after 1998's "There's Something About Mary," won the part. Her turn as Jenny has since been called one of the worst performances in any Scorsese movie.

Now, Jenny is a pretty thankless role (she's a fairly typical love interest character), but Diaz is still out of her depth. She can't keep her Irish accent down, and like Leonardo DiCaprio as Amsterdam, her wooden performance stands out all the more next to Daniel Day-Lewis' show-stopping turn as Bill the Butcher. Granted, most actors will have trouble outshining Day-Lewis (his latest film "Anemone" at least gives him a worthy scene partner in Sean Bean), but in "Gangs of New York," it's not even a competition.

That's what makes it sting to know that Sarah Michelle Gellar turned down the role. She's a great actor who carried seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" on her back. She might've still not stolen the show from Day-Lewis, but I feel confident saying she'd probably out-charisma DiCaprio's stilted Amsterdam and make Jenny a livelier character. Moreover, you can't help but wonder if Gellar's career could've soared even higher if she had a Scorsese movie on her resume.

But Gellar doesn't regret it. In 2023, she told The Guardian that she doesn't worry about the projects she missed out on due to her commitments to "Buffy," not even "Gangs of New York." This "Buffy" and Scorsese fan, though, is always going to feel a little differently.

#3547. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3546. All 4 Cillian Murphy Performances In Christopher Nolan Movies, Ranked

Like many filmmakers, Christopher Nolan often works with the same actors across different projects. Sir Michael Caine has appeared in eight Nolan films total. In second place, with room to eventually become no. 1 given Caine's retirement, is Cillian Murphy.

Murphy has acted in six films directed by Nolan, in chronological order: "Batman Begins," "The Dark Knight," "Inception," "The Dark Knight Rises," "Dunkirk," and their shared magnum opus "Oppenheimer." This prosperous creative relationship all started when Murphy auditioned to play Bruce Wayne in "Batman Begins." The two recall that they both knew Murphy wasn't the right pick for the Dark Knight, but Murphy's acting impressed Nolan enough that he fought, and won, to cast Murphy instead as one of the movie's villains: Doctor Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow.

Since then, Nolan has always known just the right way to use Murphy, to the point you could call the actor his secret weapon. Until "Oppenheimer," Murphy had never played the lead in a Nolan movie, but the director always cast him in important supporting roles (ones that needed the right actor or the whole film around them would suffer). With "Oppenheimer," Murphy carried the entire movie on his back, and his previous Nolan film performances show why he had earned the trust needed for that casting.

Even Cillian Murphy's smallest role in a Christopher Nolan movie still has meat on the bones. Nolan's World War II film "Dunkirk" depicts the 1940 evacuation of British troops from the eponymous French shoreline. Murphy plays one of those thousands of troops, specifically one whose boat gets destroyed by a German U-Boat. He's rescued by a civilian ship volunteering as a rescue boat, but taking that ride means sailing back into the carnage he just escaped.

Murphy's character doesn't even have a name, being known only as "the Shivering Soldier." Pulled from the cold water by Mr. Dawson (Mark Rylance) and boys Peter (Tom Glynn-Carney) and George (Barry Keoghan), he indeed shivers, wrapping himself in a blanket onboard. The soldier already counts himself one of the lucky ones for surviving, and he refuses to let the ship continue heading towards Dunkirk, which he believes is certain death.

With the terrifying scene the movie paints of the battle, it's hard to dismiss the soldier's fears. Peter asks if the soldier is a coward, but Mr. Dawson counters he's only shell-shocked. Murphy can pull off a thousand-yard stare like few other actors can (something he'd again do to great effect in "Oppenheimer"). That silent and haunted quality he can project makes him perfect for this part: A man who stared death in the face while watching it work all around him ... and is now being asked to do so again after getting no time to recover.

Cillian Murphy's Scarecrow is the only villain to appear in all three of the "Dark Knight Trilogy" films. During "Batman Begins," Jonathan Crane, reimagined as the head of Arkham Asylum, is in bed with both the mob and the League of Shadows, who plot to destroy Gotham City with Crane's fear toxin. Crane then returns for cameos in "The Dark Knight," being captured by Batman (Christian Bale), and "The Dark Knight Rises," serving as a judge in Bane's (Tom Hardy) kangaroo court.

Murphy is relishing playing a super-villain without ever going into pure camp territory. Though Dr. Crane admittedly isn't physically imposing, his frosty blue-eyed gaze still makes him look like a guy who can and would kill you. He's even the first villain to get one over on Batman, dosing the Dark Knight with his fear toxin and setting him on fire. Crane does the last part with a cruel quip befitting his psychologist background: "You look like a man who takes himself too seriously. Do you want my opinion? You need to lighten up."

Crane is both a sadist and a psychologist obsessed with studying the effects of fear. He relishes putting people on edge, particularly pesky crusading lawyer Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes). But Murphy's best Scarecrow scene is definitely when he pulls rank on imprisoned mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson). Murphy completely changes the tenor of the scene with Crane's line: "Would you like to see my mask?" It instantly shows Crane is not some mere corrupt bureaucrat.

Scarecrow always shows a catty sense of humor, too. So, it's fitting that his last scene in the trilogy is sentencing Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman), and others who refuse to choose between "death or exile," to "death — by exile."

In between "Dark Knight" movies, Christopher Nolan and Cillian Murphy made a little film you might've heard of called "Inception." It's a heist/con movie, but it's set inside a dreamscape. Murphy plays the dreamer and the crew's mark: Robert Fischer, the heir to an oil empire reeling from the death of his disapproving father (Pete Postlethwaite). Dominic Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his crew are hired by Fischer's rival, Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe), to plant an idea inside his head that'll make him resolve to break up his father's empire instead of inheriting it.

Speaking to Irish Central in 2010, Murphy mentioned he researched the sons of Rupert Murdoch to understand how being raised in a titan of industry's shadow would shape someone (and this was well before "Succession" gave us a Murdoch roman à clef). Murphy added that he played Fischer as "a petulant child who's in need of a lot of attention from his father." But while "Inception" is all about tricking Fischer, the movie isn't unsympathetic to him.

"Inception" is widely read as an allegory for filmmaking itself. Fischer is the audience, the one who needs to be deceived by the craft and illusion, to believe that something is real in their gut even when their brain knows it isn't. The entire movie hinges on the titular inception, where Fischer sees an illusion of his father on his deathbed and gets what life denied him: reassurance that his dad did care about him. And just as the inception has to convince Fischer, Murphy has to convince us of the emotional sincerity. An overwhelmed Fischer tears up, and as his face crumbles, it's hard not to get a lump in your own throat. It's extra painful since it's all a falsehood.

"Oppenheimer" cleaned house at the 96th Oscars, including Cillian Murphy winning Best Actor for playing the father of the atomic bomb — or, as Oppenheimer infamously called himself later in life, "death, destroyer of worlds."

On the surface, it's a transformative performance. Murphy lost weight to better capture the gaunt Oppenheimer's physique, and he completely re-modulated his voice. (Murphy based his soft but deep and rhythmic baritone as Oppenheimer on a combination of Orson Welles and Fred Rogers). But despite those hallmarks of actor transformation, the kind that often feel cynically used to win an Oscar, Murphy as Oppenheimer isn't gaudy acting. No, it's more like a chameleon shifting into a new color: Murphy becomes Oppenheimer, utterly.

"Oppie" may have been eccentric, but "Oppenheimer" is much more interested in exploring how his foibles led to his downfall — and perhaps humanity's — than venerating them as the cost of his scientific know-how. Oppenheimer is willfully naive about how the bomb he's building will be used and pathologically incapable of taking too strong a stand on anything. His equivocation often only digs him deeper. Indeed, Murphy excels in scenes that show the weighty consequences of Oppenheimer's awkwardness, like when he meets with violently anticommunist Colonel Pash (Casey Affleck) or stumbles while urging U.S. President Harry Truman (Gary Oldman) to push for nuclear de-escalation.

Oppenheimer seeking absolution from Truman by talking about the "blood on [his] hands" makes it hard to disagree with Lewis Strauss' (Robert Downey Jr.) argument that Oppenheimer wanted to be both the maker of the bomb and a martyr for its destructiveness. But in Murphy's moments of silent stillness (particularly the ending when his character imagines the world's fiery end), he shows how Oppenheimer's guilt, though self-inflicted, was all too real and impossibly heavy to carry.

#3544. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3542. Michael Fassbender's Underrated 2015 Western Is Worth Revisiting

Lots of modern Westerns take the adventurous romance out of the genre, like director John Maclean's 2015 "Slow West." A major hit at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival, it won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in the Dramatic category, and then made its way into theaters (with a simultaneous video-on-demand release). More than a decade on, "Slow West" remains one of the best Westerns of this century. And you can watch it on Netflix right now — although it's leaving soon, so act fast. It's also free, with ads, on YouTube.

"Slow West" lives up to its title with a leisurely pace, but it's also a tight 84-minute movie. In 19th century Colorado, a young Scottish man named Jay Cavendish (Kodi Smit-McPhee) sets off in search of his supposed one true love, Rose (Caren Pistorius) — who left Scotland with a price on her head. Jay meets bounty hunter Silas Selleck (Michael Fassbender) by chance and Silas becomes his guide and guardian. They also run afoul of Payne (Ben Mendelsohn), leader of a gang Silas once belonged to; Payne is interested in collecting the bounty on Rose.

Smit-McPhee later appeared in the acclaimed 2021 Western "The Power of the Dog," which similarly paired him up with Benedict Cumberbatch just as "Slow West" does with him and Fassbender. In "The Power of the Dog," Smit-McPhee is a wolf in sheep's clothing, one who weaponizes his unassuming innocence. In "Slow West," that innocence is exactly what you get with Jay Cavendish. He has naive ideas about adventure and love — Rose never actually reciprocated his feelings, but he's convinced the grand gesture of tracking her down will sway her. While the frontier forces him to defend himself with a gun, it's clear throughout the film Jay isn't built for the gunslinging life.

Jay's origins as a Scotsman traveling through America in "Slow West" are almost autobiographical for John Maclean, who is from Scotland himself. (Notably, while the parts of the film set in America were filmed in New Zealand, flashbacks to Scotland were filmed in the real country.) Speaking to the International Business Times in 2015, Maclean said how, when he first decided to write a Western, one of the first "seeds" of the story for him was to depict a frontier filled with European immigrants moving west. Jay and Rose are Scottish, Michael Fassbender uses his Irish accent to play Silas, and (without spoilers) Jay and Silas meet a Swedish family during their travels.

Unlike Jay, a newcomer to America, Maclean had seen plenty of America before making "Slow West" — which was what drew him to the Western: "After college [a few friends and I] took cars through America delivering them. So, I did a lot of traveling in America. That probably led to me wanting to do a Western."

"Slow West" was McLean's first feature film; before that, he'd been a musician and part of a group called The Beta Band, where he played keyboards and directed music videos. According to Maclean, Fassbender agreed to act in his short films because he'd been a fan of those Beta Band videos.

"He was shooting ['Inglourious Basterds'] at the time, so the fact that he even offered his services was a great thing," said Maclean to the BBC. Considering that creative partnership led to "Slow West," one of Michael Fassbender's best movies, the actor's judgment was sound.

#3541. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Beats The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim in One Major Way

After years spent dreaming of a remake or remaster of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the highest-rated video game of all time according to Metacritic, fans finally saw their wish fulfilled in 2026. Nintendo announced a remake for Switch 2 earlier this year, and the title arrived in stores this week.

Nintendo has taken some heat for relying on remakes and remasters to bolster the Switch 2 library, but time after time, they seem to delight fans and earn favorable critical reviews. Such positive performance suggests the remakes ought to continue, at least for now. It also highlights one major way Ocarina of Time beats other games that have received numerous releases over the years, such as The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim.

Depending on how you count it, Skyrim has appeared on 13 unique platforms as of November 2026, including Google Stadia (since shut down) and Amazon Alexa. There have been VR editions and bundles gathering fan-created content and expansion packs. The game originally launched on Nov. 10, 2011, and since then, it has appeared almost everywhere a large audience exists.

For its part, Ocarina of Time has appeared on far fewer platforms since its debut in 1998. That comparative rarity means each new version feels like an event, as we see with the anticipation and hype surrounding Ocarina of Time in 2026.

After it was released on the Nintendo 64, Ocarina of Time got two ports for the GameCube in North America. Nintendo included it as part of The Legend of Zelda: Collector’s Edition, a bundle of four games from the series that also included Majora’s Mask and the original NES entries, along with a demo for The Wind Waker. It also headlined a separate compilation that included the Master Quest, which previously had been available only on the Nintendo 64DD in Japan.

Next came The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D in June 2011 for the handheld Nintendo 3DS. It presented the classic adventure with quality-of-life improvements and a 3D visual effect so players could see Hyrule with extra dimension. This version also included improved texture quality throughout the adventure. If you could handle playing on a tiny screen, it was the best way to enjoy that classic version of Hyrule for years.

Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2 includes even more quality-of-life improvements, better controls, and dramatically improved visuals that incorporate an aesthetic we wouldn’t find out of place in a classic volume of fairy tales, or even in a high-end doll shop. Critics consider the game one of the year’s finest, awarding it a current Metacritic score of 96 out of 100.

There was no guarantee Nintendo could produce that result. Ocarina of Time is generally considered one of the finest games of all time, but some players find its mechanics dated. Some people just don’t like Zelda all that much. And so on, and so forth. Despite those obstacles, the development team pulled through and the result of their labor seems to be pleasing both returning fans and newcomers who have stepped into Hyrule for the very first time.

Compare that stellar reception to the one that accompanies yet another new version of Skyrim, and the difference is clear. Bethesda simply doesn’t give players time to miss the game that has accounted for more sales than any other in the company’s history. There’s always a new version of Skyrim waiting just around the corner, it seems. Perhaps we’ll even see another few editions launch before we finally get our hands on The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

New Skyrim ports usually bring genuine enhancements, but they tend to be minor if you’ve already played the original game and its expansions. Humorously, one of the most interesting versions of the game came to Nintendo hardware with Zelda-related content, starting with the Switch in November 2017. Players could dress like Link by acquiring the Champion’s Tunic, and equip themselves with the Master Sword and Hylian Shield.

I don’t mind seeing companies release multiple versions of the games players love most, because it makes them accessible to a wider audience. They also prevent me from having to haul out all my old consoles the next time I’m in a retro mood. But the slew of releases can grow tiresome when they are priced as premium titles but don’t add content or meaningful improvements. Ocarina of Time, the crown jewel in Nintendo’s library, has avoided that fate. Skyrim, the best thing Bethesda has built and launched so far, has not.

#3539. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3538. One Of Willy Wonka's Most Memorable Scenes Was An Absolute Nightmare To Shoot

Most Gen-Xers know Mel Stuart's 1971 musical movie "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory" by heart and will — perhaps recoiling in disgust — remember the scene where Augustus Gloop (Michael Böllner) falls into a river of chocolate. It seems that moment was equally revolting to film.

The scene in question occurs about halfway through the movie, by which point Willy Wonka (Gene Wilder) has opened the doors to his ultra-secretive chocolate factory to five sweepstakes-winning children. Wonka is a zany eccentric who seems to grow rare and exotic chocolate plants that produce fully manufactured candy. One of the first stops on the factory tour is a stroll through his candy garden, and the contest winners are allowed to feast on all the unusual edible flora their stomachs can handle. This sequence alone makes "Willy Wonka" one of the best food movies of all time.

Running through the middle of the garden is Wonka's chocolate river. He explains that a river is the best way to keep chocolate mixed, and it is the one thing that is verboten to touch. It should be noted that the chocolate river, from a production standpoint, looks more like mud or sewage than chocolate. It's watery and unappealing. Augustus, however, cannot help spooning some of the chocolate river into his mouth. He then slips and falls into the water, splashing around for a bit before being sucked into a drainage pipe.

According to Polygon's 2021 oral history of this scene, that river was as gross in person as it looked on camera. Böllner recalled having to film this moment for a long stretch, forcing him to repeatedly fall into, in his words, "stinky water." Also, it was cold. So, much less fun that actually swimming in liquid chocolate.

Michael Böllner added that he had to fall into a deep aperture under the water every time he dove into the river. The aperture, however, wasn't very large, and he repeatedly risked slamming his head into the solid river floor. As he put it:

"It was actually not chocolate. It was terribly cold. It was stinky water! And it was all day long, jumping in and jumping out, and being around with wet clothes. [...] The river was just 10 centimeters deep. And there was a hole about a square meter that I had to hit. So, I was very scared that I would not hit the square meter and would punch my head in the ground of the chocolate river."

Böllner didn't say what, exactly, the river smelled like, but its brackish, near-translucent brown might make one suspect that it was colored with paint. Julie Dawn Cole, who played the spoiled Veruca Salt in "Willy Wonka," also recalled poor Böllner's experience falling into that river all day. According to her, the water was not the least bit fresh, remaining stagnant for weeks. What's more, it seems that the film's cast and/or crew kept using it as a means of disposing of their drinks (which may very well explain the odor):

"Michael had to fall into this disgusting stuff that had been sitting there for three weeks. It had the lights on it, and people were emptying their coffee cup dregs into it."

So, Böllner had to splash into an unseen trough covered by three-week-old brown coffee water. Movie magic!

At the end of the chocolate river scene, Augustus, as mentioned, is sucked up a transparent pipe. His body blocks the pipe, though, and one can see his screaming face through the glass while chocolate pressure builds up beneath him. To film this moment, Michael Böllner had to be lowered into a tube, about six feet long in actuality, that was then filled with chocolate water. Naturally, Böllner did not enjoy this, either, explaining:

"It was a really tough thing because they took about two meters tube around me and filled it up with water up to my mouth. So, I couldn't move anything. I couldn't do anything. I just had to rely on the guys that were around me that don't drop me."

Peter Ostrum, who played Charlie Bucket, the protagonist of "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," also commented on the whole river scene, recalling that it looked utterly miserable. He knew the water was cold and gross, so he was merely relieved he didn't have to do the stunt himself. To quote him directly:

"When I saw Michael do take after take after take of falling in the cold river, that cold, dirty river, I just thought, 'I'm glad that's him and not me!'"

Indeed, this scene is but one of many reasons why folks of a certain age remember "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" as being delightful nightmare fuel. That and Willy Wonka is quite the twisted trickster in the film (something you can partly thank Gene Wilder himself for). As for its young stars, they all largely went on to enjoy various careers outside of acting. Luckily, none of them ever had to deal with brackish fake rivers again.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3536. 39 Years Later, Inigo Montoya's Princess Bride Line Is Still The Greatest Movie Quote Ever

Do you love big, sweeping, epic romances where the lovers are kept apart for years, only to reunite in a scene that takes your breath away? Do you love clever, quippy, dialogue? Do you love swashbuckling adventures with a touch of vengeance? Great news. "The Princess Bride" has literally all of those things.

In 1987, writer-director Rob Reiner released "The Princess Bride," an adaptation of William Goldman's novel of the same name — and with Goldman adapting his own work into the screenplay, every second isn't just true to the book, but elevates the material. Robin Wright made her feature film debut as Princess Buttercup, a lovelorn woman who mourns the apparent loss of her one true love, a stable boy named Westley (Cary Elwes), and, believing him dead, agrees to marry the horrible Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon). Elsewhere, swordsman Inigo Montoya (Mandy Patinkin), who always travels with the friendly giant Fezzik (André the Giant), wants revenge on the man who killed his father, and when Westley reappears as the Dread Pirate Roberts, he ends up teaming up with Inigo and Fezzik to also rescue Buttercup. Wallace Shawn, Carol Kane, and Billy Crystal play pivotal supporting roles in this film. It's basically perfect.

If you've seen "The Princess Bride" — and the odds are that you have — you know it's chock-a-block full of quotable lines. Today, though, we're celebrating one of its most beloved and well-known quotes, 39 years after its release.

Throughout "The Princess Bride," Mandy Patinkin's dashing and skilled swordsman Inigo Montoya has one goal: to find the six-fingered man who killed his father when Inigo was just a boy. For years, Inigo has been searching for this specific killer to avenge his dear old dad — and he finds him in the film in the form of Count Tyrone Rugen (Christopher Guest). So why is this line so important to the film, and why is it so beloved after nearly four decades?

For one thing, Inigo says it, like, 80 times in the movie, so it's easy to remember. It's a testament to Rob Reiner's sharp, exacting sense of comedic timing that the line never loses any luster, but remains funny every single time Patinkin delivers it (which is also a credit to Patinkin, a truly formidable performer who's been excellent for generations at this point). It's also connected to the movie's enduring message of love, even though it definitely seems a little more murdery than the flowery declarations of passion exchanged between Westley and Buttercup. Inigo truly loved his father, and once he kills the genuinely evil Rugen, the character delivers a line that defined Patinkin's actual life.

Reiner, who was tragically killed alongside his wife Michele Singer Reiner in late 2025 at his home in Los Angeles, made movies with big jokes and even bigger hearts. This line perfectly exemplifies that, and across the board, "The Princess Bride" is one of his very best films. So what other "Princess Bride" quotes stand the test of time?

Wordle is a daily word-guessing game that tasks players with solving a five-word puzzle using letter position clues. Wordle presents the player with six rows of five empty boxes. Simply enter a random five-letter word and the website highlights certain letters in green if they are correct, yellow if they are correct but in the wrong spot, or grey if they are not in the word at all. With this information, players need to try to figure out the word within the six guesses to be successful.

These types of guessing games have been around for a long time. One of the originals was called Mastermind, where players are tasked with guessing a row of colored pegs that utilizes the same hint systems found in Wordle. If players would like to try the game for themselves, it can be found on the Wordle website, which creates a new puzzle every day, keeps track of players' win streaks and guess distribution, and has a popular sharing ability.

#3533. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3532. Set Phasers To Stun: Star Trek's Different Phaser Settings Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

When Gene Roddenberry was first assembling "Star Trek" in the mid-1960s, the term "laser guns" was common enough sci-fi parlance that he astutely wanted to avoid using it. To make "Star Trek" seem a little more futuristic, Roddenberry invented "phasers" instead of "lasers," and the weapon became a staple of the franchise. Starfleet vessels are equipped with powerful phaser weapons used for ship-to-ship combat, and Starfleet officers carry hand-held phasers into potentially dangerous situations.

In the pilot episode for "Star Trek: Enterprise," a series set a century prior to the events of the original "Star Trek," Captain Archer (Scott Bakula) was shown a hand-held phaser — then called a phase pistol — for the first time, so Starfleet has been using them since the very start. Phasers tend to fire single, confined beams, but would also eventually come to fire brief, bullet-like pulses.

"Star Trek," however, is also meant to take place in a peaceful utopia, so the phasers were said to have a "stun" setting that could render an attacker unconscious from a distance. Only in extreme scenarios would a phaser be adjusted to the "kill" setting, which could blast the life out of someone. Indeed, throughout "Star Trek," the powerful kill setting was seen to vaporize a person's body entirely.

On "Enterprise," phasers only had "stun" and "kill" settings, but later on, there were other, gentler settings. Throughout the franchise, characters have been explicit about the various settings a hand phaser was capable of using, sometimes referring to "light stun," "heavy stun," or a numerical system.

What do those numbers and settings mean? Let's take a look.

Eagle-eyed "Star Trek" viewers might notice that Starfleet officers typically use two different types of phasers. The Type-1 phasers are the smaller, thumb-activated, remote-control-looking widgets, while the larger, pistol-shaped phasers are Type-2. On "Next Generation," the Type-2 also became a thumb-operated device. Only very occasionally would one see a larger phaser rifle, like the one Captain Kirk (William Shatner) used in the episode "Where No Man Has Gone Before."

In the "Star Trek: Discovery" episode "Saints of Imperfection," Tilly (Mary Wiseman) also noted that the rifle is designated a Type-3 weapon by saying, "It is more powerful and generally larger than the Type-1 or Type-2, which I guess is why they call it a 3."

The original phaser sound effect, a high-pitched whine, was repurposed from the 1953 film "The War of the Worlds." The common "Star Trek" phaser sound has remained a variant of that whine ever since.

It was in the episode "The Enemy Within" that "setting one," a phaser's lowest setting, was first mentioned. This was enough to, well, stun the average humanoid. In the episode "The Return of the Archons," the Enterprise crew set their phasers to a wide-beam setting that could essentially spray across a crowd, stunning multiple people at once. (It's a good thing I don't have a phaser with a wide-beam setting; I would never wait in line for a ride at Disneyland ever again.)

On "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine," specifically in the episode "Homefront," there was some mention that setting 3.5 or 3.6 constituted a "heavy stun." It wouldn't be until a phaser was set to setting 10 that it would be capable of vaporizing someone. Starfleet seems more interested in gradations of stunning someone before it considers a kill setting ... but those puppies can do a lot of damage.

In the "Next Generation" episode "Frame of Mind," Riker (Jonathan Frakes) has a scene where he sets a Type-2 phaser to its maximum setting of 16. He states out loud that if a phaser were to fire at such a setting, it would destroy half the building. Phasers, if wielded irresponsibly, could apparently do a great deal of damage. Of course, these are hand-held devices and don't have an infinite power supply. I think it's safe to assume that a phaser, firing a level-16 blast, could only do it once. I'd hate to live in a world where someone could stroll through a city, blasting open multiple buildings willy-nilly with a single handgun-sized object.

A stun setting could knock someone out without leaving a mark, but, judging by various makeup jobs seen throughout "Star Trek," heavier settings left bruises or even burn marks on people. Before you think you could withstand a heavy stun, watch one of those foolish online videos where macho idiots — or perhaps just the cast members of the "Jackass" crew — test to see if they can withstand a taser or pepper spray. I imagine a phaser blast would be the sci-fi version of that.

Of course, throughout "Star Trek," officers also used phasers for things other than tactical confrontations. They could be used as cutting torches, or to heat up rocks in order to keep warm in frozen climates. In the "Next Generation" episode "Disaster," a phaser's power cell was used as a power source for a computer terminal. Phasers may have the ability to explode entire buildings, but they are more often used as tools in a Starfleet officer's toolbox.

#3531. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s revamped StandBy to other iPhones

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in December. To learn more about StandBy and how to customize its different faces, follow this link.

#3530. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3529. James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009

James Gray time-travels back to his Queens roots once again for his latest film, “Paper Tiger.” It’s a location, an atmosphere, a state of mind he’s explored across decades and genres, dating back to his 1994 debut feature, “Little Odessa.” Like “Paper Tiger,” “Little Odessa” also featured the shadows of the Russian mafia looming over a family unit — to devastating ends. But even 30-plus years later, with his new movie — starring Miles Teller, Adam Driver, and Scarlett Johansson — Gray wanted to go just as dangerous.

Adam Driver, for one, has danger in him, according to Gray, who cast the Oscar nominee as a former police officer who links up with the red mafia in the 1980s. Gray recently joined IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio for a wide-ranging, amusingly discursive live conversation at the Virginia Film Festival. One that showcased his knack for impressions — from Luca Guadagnino beckoning Gray out of this year’s Cannes to sit down for the Italian filmmaker’s Bernardo Bertolucci documentary, to the waves of disappointment cresting through Maximilian Schell during an early Venice screening of “Little Odessa.” Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Almost all great performances have to have some measure of danger in them,” Gray said. “I can actually only think of one that doesn’t have any, which would probably be Jeff Bridges as The Dude in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ which has no danger at all.” (Though John Goodman’s PTSD-addled Vietnam vet in the Coens’ 1998 hardboiled slacker comedy qualifies as dangerous.)

“Adam is a fantastic, intense presence in [‘Paper Tiger’],” said Gray, who wrote “Paper Tiger” with Driver in mind.

Gray also spoke about the “recurring nightmares” for any filmmaker: “You screen your movie, and everybody walks out midway through. I’ve never had that happen to me, thank God.”

But one personal experience of watching this happen to someone else became seared in his unconscious: “When I was on the jury in Cannes [in 2009] … there was a movie made by a fantastic director. I won’t say his name, but he’s a great director of real reputation. And you have to sit in this jury box, which is sort of in the back of a theater, and the seats … when a person gets up, it’s spring-activated, and so it makes this very loud tack. I’m on the jury, and I’m watching this movie, and I start hearing tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack. And people start walking out in droves. And the movie ended, and it was about half full, and people were booing. And that did become a nightmare for me. And by the way, I’m not the only director for whom that’s a nightmare. I’ve talked to many director friends of mine, and they’re like, ‘Oh, yeah. No, I’ve had that dream.'”

James Gray served on the Cannes jury in 2009 under president Isabelle Huppert — whom he reiterated, as Huppert previously did with IndieWire, he has no feud with despite rumors of a fractious deliberation — with such films as Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void” and Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist” in the competition. (But again, he’s not naming names here.)

“I know there’s directors who go, ‘I like it. I like when they boo,’ but that’s such a crock,” said Gray. We also asked for his thoughts on audiences dozing off in movies — which some directors, like Lucrecia Martel, have likened to falling asleep in the sun, a reflex of comfort — which certainly happens with some frequency at Cannes as any attendee knows.

“Who likes when you fall asleep during a movie? No, I’m sorry. The movie is required to keep you awake, and as Hitchcock once said, it has to be just long enough to accommodate your bladder’s capacity,” Gray said. “Which, by the way, you know when people say, ‘Oh, well, what do you think of the streaming thing and all that?’ I have only one real beef with streaming, and that’s the pause button, because it is my job to keep you there for an hour and a half, two hours, maybe even three. Where you’re not falling asleep, where you are riveted, where you’re not moving.”

He added, “I can’t stand the people who go, ‘I watched the first half on Tuesday, but I’m gonna catch the second half on a Saturday.’ … There’s nothing you can do about it, and it’s not, it’s not streamer-centered, because most people watch your films now at home. And whether it’s Netflix or Peacock or whatever, it doesn’t matter. The pause button is a problem.”

He pointed to his early relationship to “Vertigo,” a Hitchcock film he didn’t like in the first half, as an example of the virtues of experiencing a movie entirely in one sitting. “The result is so much more rewarding when you are forced to experience the whole thing because it’s like a dream, and you can’t pause your dream. And sometimes you don’t like your dream … sometimes the only way you can get yourself out of that dream is to convince yourself it is a dream in your dream. REM sleep is an hour and a half to two hours a night. What’s a movie’s runtime? It’s about the same thing. It didn’t happen by accident,” Gray said.
