#3505. 6 Superhero Characters Who Work Best on TV

With how prevalent superheroes have become in movies and television over the decades, it's become more and more clear that some heroes work better in one medium over another. This isn't to say that because a hero works in one medium, they can't work in another, but there are some that simply thrive more in television or movies, respectively.

Television has proven to be a great outlet for superhero storytelling, thanks to how much time a character gets to spend with the audience. Whether it be because their world is simply best executed on a smaller television budget, they have more day-to-day storytelling, or benefit from spending more time with an audience than the average bear, superhero TV is sometimes the best medium for some heroes. These characters prove exactly why that can be.

While the Disney+ television era of the Marvel Cinematic Universe had its fair share of complaints, there are still some series that people liked, and one of them is, without a doubt, Moon Knight. While—thanks to his mythology and power set—one might initially think that he would actually fit better on the big screen, Marvel's white-clad superhero has already proven why he works better on television. When a character isn't massively known by general audiences, sometimes they actually benefit more from being a show because audiences get to spend more time with them and can grow more attached to them than they could in just two hours.

Over the course of Disney+'s Moon Knight, viewers got to spend almost six hours with Oscar Isaac's iconic hero, getting them attached to him better than they ever could have before. It's gotten to the point that people are begging to see him in other Marvel content now because of it. There's also a hefty dose of mystery and lore to uncover in the hero's mythological roots and the many unexplored corners of his mind, and the way it's covered over the many hours of the series couldn't have been done in a movie. It's actually pretty safe to say that Moon Knight would not have worked as well as a movie, making the character genuinely better-suited for television.

Sometimes a lot of it comes down to budget management, and that is most definitely the case with Green Arrow. Because of the character not having superpowers and being a bow and arrow-wielding hero, far less budget is necessary for bringing the Emerald Archer to life than others—even the likes of other non-powered heroes like Batman. While they could make a Green Arrow movie and do some cool stuff within it because of the less budget needed for the hero, executing his stories on television ends up being the better move, with no question.

He's already been a success on TV, actually, via the CW's Arrow (despite being more of a Batman show than a Green Arrow show). Why use the extra budget leftover from not needing to execute superpowers for a 2-hour story, when one could use that extra budget across an entire season of a show? This would allow the studios to do more on a week-to-week basis, rather than a one-time go in theaters. Not to mention, the hero's stories aren't usually gigantic world-ending threats that require the kind of budget a typical superhero movie has. Again, it becomes a case of being able to simply do more on television than they could in a film.

If it isn't already obvious, the one and only Invincible (Steven Yeun) has quickly become one of the most prominent television superheroes of all time. The show is already adapting the book very accurately, and people are adoring it. So . . . why is there a movie in development? This is a question that has rested on the minds of fans for quite some time, because everyone can agree that the show is pretty much the best medium for the series.

Invincible is already adapting the entire comic book run—so long as they go for the amount of seasons they want to—so the concept of doing him in a movie feels a bit redundant. There's simply no question that Invincible is already the best of what an adaptation of the series could be, so it warrants the title of this character working best on television. Why even try to fix something that's not broken?

This character has already starred in an animated television show—Static Shock—and it was exceptional. This is primarily because the protagonist, Virgil Hawkins (Phil LaMarr), is a very grounded, street-level hero. He's just a 16-year-old kid who's trying to do his best—a Spider-Man-esque character, in a way. Coming-of-age stories are great, and there are plenty of coming-of-age movies, but this genre on television can often be far more effective.

Getting to spend a decent amount of time with a character who's growing so much into the person they're going to be—like Virgil is, on a superpowered scale—allows the audience to really gravitate towards and fall in love with the protagonist. It also gives viewers time to really explore the hero's world and dive into the characters that surround him, fleshing out his journey into a whole new depth.

Four people, four completely different ideas of what it means to have somebody in your corner. Here is who picked up, what they would ask of you, and what you would get back.

You want the friend who does not leave. Steve is the one who turns up at the door without being asked, who remembers what you said you were worried about, and who has never once made you audition for his attention.

You want the friend who is genuinely exhausting and completely worth it. Tony will forget your birthday, then build you something at four in the morning that you did not know you needed, and hand it over as though it were nothing.

You want the friend who replies in four seconds and apologises for it. Peter is earnest in a way that is almost unfashionable, and he will take on far more than he can carry rather than admit that he is struggling.

You want the friend who insults your shoes, fixes your phone and then quietly rearranges your entire life for the better. Shuri does not do soft reassurance, and that is the reason you would believe her when she says you are fine.

One of the most famous and beloved Marvel television shows is the one and only Daredevil—no contest. The televised story of Matt Murdock (Charlie Cox) has become so popular that people begged for the show and the actor to return, leading to the announcement of the sequel series, Daredevil: Born Again. The Netflix series is genuinely considered a true work of art.

This character is much like a lot of other television-preferred superheroes in the fact that he is a street-level hero, and far more grounded than others. This makes it far easier to depict him on television, and having the extra time for viewers to watch him makes the political thriller and mystery aspects of the show have so much more time to be more complex than they ever could have been in just a movie.

Despite Spider-Man: Brand New Day being within the top three highest-grossing movies of all time, the character of Spider-Man is easily better suited for television. The best parts about the character are the coming-of-age aspects of his journey, his gigantic group of supporting characters, and even larger catalog of villains. Sure, these things are adapted very well to film—the large number of massively successful films being prooof—but his stories told on television can often be considered some of the best adaptations of the character, period.

A great example of this is the likes of The Spectacular Spider-Man—a series that has episodes that can genuinely be considered masterpieces—and Spider-Man: The Animated Series. These are noted by many to be some of the best iterations of the character ever put onto screen, and that's not for no reason. The huge amount of time audiences have spent with these versions of the character makes for a connection unlike any other. Not to mention, the fact that they're animated means they have no restrictions when it comes to bringing certain characters to life—limitless potential for comic accurate designs and unique powers—and allows for some amazing spectacle.

#3503. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3502. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3501. It's Officially The End Of An Era For The Arrowverse

The news that there are not one, but two new Constantine movies reportedly in the works means that Matt Ryan’s underrated Arrowverse take on the Alan More character will soon no longer be the most recent screen version of the iconic antihero. Based on DC's Hellblazer comic book series, 2005’s Constantine starred Keanu Reeves as the eponymous dour demon slayer, an exorcist cursed with the ability to communicate, and fight, with both angels and demons alike.

With slick direction from future I Am Legend director Francis Lawrence and an incredible cast that included Djimon Hounsou, Shia LaBeouf, Tilda Swinton, Peter Stormare, and The Mummy franchise’s Rachel Weisz as the title character’s femme fatale love interest, Constantine was an early R-rated comic book movie that did justice to co-creators Stephen R. Bissette and Alan Moore’s character. However, although Constantine 2 is set to happen eventually, it is not the definitive screen take on the character.

Matt Ryan was cast as John Constantine in 2014’s NBC series Constantine, a dark thriller that took Supernatural’s fun and From Dusk Til Dawn’s edge to make a memorably creepy comic book adaptation. Sadly, Constantine lasted a mere 13 episodes before the series was canceled, but, fortunately, this was not the end of Ryan’s take on the character. In the years that followed, the Arrowverse adopted Ryan’s Constantine, and he appeared in Arrow, Legends of Tomorrow, Batwoman, The Flash, and Harley Quinn.

While Ryan's Constantine also starred in the web series Constantine: City of Demons, it is the iconic DC series Legends of Tomorrow that really warrants further discussion here. Ryan's Constantine was in one episode each other Arrow, Batwoman, The Flash, and Harley Quinn, whereas the actor appeared in a grand total of 47 episodes of Legends of Tomorrow when his recurring season 3 role was fleshed out into a major main role from seasons 4–6.

For those keeping count, that meant that Ryan appeared in almost three times as many Legend of Tomorrow episodes as he did episodes of Constantine itself. The star became one of the highlights of the Arrowverse, while the Arrowverse itself gave Ryan's take on the character of Constantine a whole new lease of life in return. However, after a 12-year reign, Ryan will soon no longer be the most recent live-action version of the character.

Recently, Deadline reported that Evil Dead Wrath's Francis Galluppi is working on a script for another Constantine movie for DC. Seemingly unrelated to the Reeves movie's long-gestating sequel, this movie means that although there could soon be two Constantine live-action movies happening, neither would bring back the Arrowverse’s version of the character.

The fact that HBO made a new version of Watchmen a mere ten years after director Zack Snyder’s take on the iconic graphic novel means Moore is no stranger to seeing his work adapted repeatedly. However, Ryan’s unique trajectory with the character of Constantine, from his swiftly canceled show to joining the Arrowverse, to his long run on Legends of Tomorrow, was a truly chaotic and unpredictable one.

For a long stretch of Legends of Tomorrow, Ryan even ended up playing a different character because DC seemingly had plans for Constantine back then. Of course, these plans never amounted to anything, which meant Ryan could then reprise the role for the DC Animated Movie Universe. However, this also seems to bode badly for the upcoming live-action movie.

From the brevity of Ryan’s show to the long wait for Reeves’ sequel, Constantine seems to be a character that Hollywood has a hard time nailing down. As such, perhaps fans of the Arrowverse need not worry too much after all, as it might still be a while before this proposed Constantine movie actually materializes.

#3499. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3498. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3497. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

#3494. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

why are people defending Apple? They are bending everybody over double to keep their profit margins. They buy a billion memory chips or SSD's at a time so they are getting them much lower in price even if the price has gone up.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

#3492. Project Hail Mary's Wisest Quote Is Already One Of The Greatest Lines In Modern Sci-Fi History

Katrina joined ScreenRant as a news writer in 2024, covering box office, expert interviews, exclusives, and new releases. Her work has appeared in CBR, All About Jazz, Rising Artists, and numerous other publications. She has an MFA in Creative Writing and has published more than 20 books. She currently writes for ScreenRant’s movie features team.

Since its theatrical release in March 2026, Phil Lord and Chris Miller's movie adaptation of Andy Weir's Project Hail Mary has received a lot of praise from critics and audiences alike. With a near-perfect Rotten Tomatoes score, the sci-fi pic is a recent standout in the genre.

From Ryan Gosling's performance to Grace and Rocky's friendship, the movie has many memorable moments. Great quotes and funny banter resonate well with fans.

While Rocky and Grace's cross-species friendship takes most of the spotlight, the movie's deeply human take on space adventure is what makes it special, and one line, in particular, is the heart of the movie. Project Hail Mary's wisest line isn't in the loudest scene, but it happens to be one of the best lines in recent sci-fi history.

Project Hail Mary's wisest quote comes fairly early in the movie. When Captain Yao assumed that Grace would join the mission if asked, Grace admitted that he would choose not to do it because he lacked courage. Captain Yao then told him that everyone is capable of courage, and they just need to find the person that makes them brave, which, in retrospect, is what the movie is about.

"Anyone can be brave. You just need someone to be brave for." — Captain Yao

Grace spent the first half of the movie trying to decode the lives of his fellow crew. He admired their courage for giving their lives on Earth for the mission and felt the weight of the mission, but he didn't fully understand the meaning of sacrifice until he met Rocky.

Gosling's schoolteacher is far from what a brave man looks like on the outside. Unlike the other astronauts on his team, he said no to joining the mission and was involuntarily put into a coma so that he could make a much-needed continued contribution to the human race. His moment of bravery came later in the film when he chose to save Rocky instead of going back to Earth.

For Grace, saving humanity is a big concept that comes with responsibilities and commitment, which sounds like something that only heroes do, but saving Rocky is simple. All he had to do was show up. Captain Yao's quote decodes big concepts such as heroism, sacrifices, and bravery into basic human experiences and ordinary courage that everyone is capable of. The fact that the line was delivered in a rather ordinary scene makes it even more meaningful.

While on the surface, Project Hail Mary tells a story about space adventures and making contact with extraterrestrial lifeforms; the movie investigates Grace's relationship with courage. Captain Yao gave Grace the answer before the school teacher-turned-astronaut fully understood the meaning, and in doing so, it created a powerful echo effect.

From 2001: A Space Odyssey to Jeremy Renner's Arrival and the critically acclaimed Annihilation that stars Natalie Portman in the lead role, many of the best sci-fi flicks use speculative concepts to examine the human condition. Christopher Nolan's epic sci-fi pic Interstellar uses the concept of a wormhole and time dilation to explore love and survival. Similarly, Project Hail Mary approaches time dilation and extraterrestrial life by asking what makes a person courageous and what makes life worth fighting for.

Project Hail Mary rejects the default assumption that only heroes rise to the occasion and that some of us are born courageous. Instead of offering a familiar speech about bravery, Captain Yao's words make it personal.

Grace eventually found the person he'd be brave for in space. They may not speak the same language or come from the same planet, but they're both the sole survival engineers on the same mission to save their planet, and they would do everything, including putting their lives at risk, to save one another.

Rocky and Grace's friendship grounds the scientific aspects of Project Hail Mary in the very things that make human experiences meaningful, which are love, family, and friendship.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

The doctors at the local neurology center suspect that she might be suffering from the early symptoms of a brain tumor, but Zi — a being of pure cinema, cobbled together from the half-formed memories of films like “La Jetée” and “Cléo from 5 to 7” — will have to wait a long and lonely 24 hours for the test results to come back.  Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

Well, maybe not so lonely. Crying on one of the innumerable concrete steps that climb Lantau Island, Zi is consoled by a sweet American expat with a strangely familiar face (and an aggressively unnatural blonde wig). Her name is L, she’s a disillusioned former dancer played by the luminous Haley Lu Richardson, and she can’t help but reciprocate the inexplicable closeness that Zi feels towards her. Over the course of a single night together, these two lost souls will help to relocate each other in time — to resynchronize with the world around them, reconnect with the infinite potential of the present, and return themselves to the creative purpose that once anchored them to it.

Even if seen without a shred of context, it would be obvious to anyone that “Zi” was made by someone who is — or hopefully was — desperate to spark a realignment of his own. To steal himself away from regret and anxiety and tether his perspective back to the now. Shot without a script or a budget in the immediate aftermath of Kogonada’s ill-received “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” (the “After Yang” auteur’s studio debut, by all indications a soul-crushing experience for an artist whose two previous features retained the delicate grace of the video essays that he used to make), this searching and unformed wisp of an experiment hardly represents the first time that an ascendent director has scaled down after a misstep, but “Zi” takes the notion of “one for me” to much greater and more galvanizing extremes than usual.

This isn’t just a filmmaker trying to get back on track, it’s a filmmaker desperately, nakedly searching for a way to fall back in love with filmmaking itself. A way to prove that it might still love him back. (Kogonada described the project to IndieWire as “A retreat, as well as a pursuit.”)

While the prospect of watching Kogonada do that will naturally be of greater interest to those who have watched him get to this point, this movie’s palpably improvised nature — its stolen shots and recursive shape lend the impression of someone trying to cut their ultra-evocative vacation footage into a coherent narrative — would force anyone to wonder about the meta-textual aspects of its creation. “You feel like your sole purpose in life is something, and it doesn’t choose you back,” L sputters out at one point. “What do you do with that? I had to get away from it all. That’s why I came here. Wandering.”

Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed.

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present.

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals.

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes.

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3487. The MCU’s Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

The MCU is the most successful film franchise in Hollywood history, giving us countless memorable moments — action sequences, quotable scenes, character interactions filled with poignancy and humor, etc. — over the course of its 70+ projects. With such a wealth of options, any argument to be made for one such moment standing as the best in the franchise is likely to be challenged. Oddly enough, being "challenged" just so happens to be the impetus behind the quote that we assert is the greatest in the franchise's history. It's a line that applies to the franchise both on and off the screen, and it's been said more than once by one of the original Avengers, Captain America (Chris Evans), over the course of the franchise's history: "I can do this all day."

The quote is said by Steve Rogers four times over the course of the MCU franchise, with two of those in the film that brought the character into the MCU: Captain America: The First Avenger. The first instance occurs prior to Rogers being given the super serum, where the small and scrawny Rogers is getting beaten up in an alleyway. The attacker is the loud jerk (credited as the "Loud Jerk") Rogers yells at to stop talking during a wartime newsreel shown before a movie. It's no contest: the man is much bigger, and pummels Rogers relentlessly. Only Rogers refuses to stay down, defiantly standing back up and uttering, "I can do this all day."

He can't, or at least shouldn't, but he does, with the words capturing the fighting spirit that refuses to give up, whatever the odds; a spirit that made Rogers the perfect recipient of the serum. So when he says it the next time, during his fight with Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), the quote rings differently. Rogers now has the strength to carry it through, changing the quote from one of admirable defiance to a rallying cry.

The line rings differently, yet again, the third time Rogers says it, during the final one-on-one fight against Iron Man (Robert Downey Jr.) in Captain America: Civil War. Now it's a statement as to how far he'll go to stick to his morals and beliefs, challenging Tony Stark not only physically but ideally, refusing to back down from either. And when we catch up with Rogers after the events of Avengers: Infinity War in Avengers: Endgame, the same drive represented by "I can do this all day" is routed in a different, compassionate way, with Rogers turning his full attention to helping those left behind. And when his 2012 self says the quote later in the film during the fight with his 2023 self, knowing what the quote means makes the moment quite funny, with the two both unwilling to back down.

The strongest challenger for MCU's greatest quote is arguably "I am Iron Man" — the line that, for all intents and purposes, began and ended the MCU's Infinity Saga. Only it applies almost exclusively to the man who said it, Tony Stark, and charts his progression from egotist to self-sacrificing hero, whereas "I can do this all day" goes beyond Steve Rogers to apply to the franchise as a whole. Time and again, the protagonists of the MCU refuse to back down from whoever, or whatever, they're up against. The stand to protect New York from the Chitauri in The Avengers. The final battle against Thanos (Josh Brolin) and his overwhelming army in Avengers: Endgame. Confronting the massive, mighty Galactus (Ralph Ineson), despite the four Fantastics together being smaller than his pinky, in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. And so much more.

Offscreen, the phrase serves as a meta joke of sorts for the MCU, a franchise that has mirrored Captain America's arc, from a scrawny Steve franchise to what it is today. With Avengers: Doomsday set to extend the franchise's dominance at the movie theater, it's easy to picture Kevin Feige saying those exact words. Through the highs of Avengers: Endgame to the lows of Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, the MCU keeps standing up again, defiant. So long as the fans continue to come out, to see films that deserve to be seen (sorry, Eternals), Feige and company absolutely can, and will, "do this all day."

#3486. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3485. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

I’m okay with Apple doing this. HOWEVER, they should publish at least rough guidelines on what they will consider “harmful”.

Saying nothing more than “harmful” leaves way too much open to arbitrary interpretation.

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3484. John Carpenter Cult Classic Officially Returns On November 12

John Carpenter, the master of horror, has created several phenomenal cult classic films that fans continue to delight in (perhaps with their hands ever so slightly covering their eyes) to this very day. From The Thing to Halloween and everything in between, Carpenter's numerous classics have become staples in the world of cinema, worthy of academic study, of enjoying relaxed in a recliner with a cold beverage and a bowl of popcorn, or in their updated and transformed forms as video games, board games, and multimedia experiences.

However you consume your Carpenter flicks, there's no denying that they rank among some of the very best, especially in the world of horror. Fortunately, one John Carpenter's greatest works is making a splashy return. Fans of this particular experience are undoubtedly going to get a kick out of this latest project, if they haven't already, and newcomers will be introduced to the fascinating and slightly terrifying mind of one of cinema's greatest directors.

John Carpenter's Toxic Commando was released back in March 2026 to positive reviews, offering fans a thrilling first-person horde shooter that aimed to replace the likes of Left 4 Dead, or at least deliver a compelling alternative to it. It did everything it needed to, its main flaw being that it released during a wave of similarly designed first-person shooters, and thus struggled to find as big an audience as it may have done a few years prior. Of course, Toxic Commando isn't Carpenter's first foray into video games, but it does prove to be his most accessible game yet.

That works in its favor, however, as it makes it a prime target for a relatively easy comeback, something that may very well be possible now that it is launching on Xbox Game Pass. Joining the pantheon of great co-op games on Game Pass, Toxic Commando looks set to see a flurry of new players experience its chaotic horde-based gameplay. It was inevitable that it would eventually grace the platform, if only due to its multiplayer focus facilitating a constant cycle of new players, something that Game Pass is more than capable of delivering.

John Carpenter's Toxic Commando is coming to Xbox Game Pass and PC Game Pass on November 12. It will likely stay on the platform for a year or so, giving players plenty of time to dive headfirst into its visceral first-person shooting with a few friends. If you are interested, John Carpenter's Toxic Commando sees up to four players head into large open levels with assorted goals and objectives to complete, not unlike the aforementioned Left 4 Dead 2. However, there are huge Space Marine 2-esque hordes of zombies and mutants that will quickly overwhelm you if you're not careful.

John Carpenter's Toxic Commando can be played solo with AI-controlled teammates that do a decent job of assisting the player

Toxic Commando marked John Carpenter's move away from Hollywood, as it is an original video game not based on any of his previous work. It was still written and scored by the director, however, and thus features all of his trademark quirks that made his films so special. It ultimately proves to be a cinematic yet deeply video gamey experience that is well worth playing if you're a fan of his work. If you've been looking for a new co-operative shooter and overlooked John Carpenter's Toxic Commando when it first came out, then now is the time to play it.
